numpy-arrays.title: When One Calculation Needed to Work on Many Measurements

sources.title: Harris and colleagues: Array programming with NumPy (2020)
Python: lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries

blocks: Scientific programs often repeat the same operation on long collections of measurements. Writing a separate instruction for every reading makes the program harder to inspect, while writing a Python loop for every numerical operation can add overhead.

The NumPy authors' 2020 account describes an array model that combines compact expressions with compiled numerical operations. The useful idea for us is simple: organise the readings once, then express a calculation for the collection. Our greenhouse readings are invented, not measurements from that paper.

numpy-axes.title: Keeping the Meaning of a Scientific Table

sources.title: Python: lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries

blocks: Scientific records commonly separate observations from the things measured about them. Array programming keeps those distinctions as axes, so a calculation can combine one direction while preserving the others.

NumPy's documented reduction operations make the chosen axis explicit. Our two-day greenhouse table is an invented example of why that choice matters. We are using an established array convention, not attributing the invention of tables or averages to NumPy.

numpy-creation.title: When the Layout Was Known Before the Measurements
blocks: Scientific programs often know the dimensions of a calculation before they have its results. They need storage for accumulators, trial settings, and numerical grids without writing each entry by hand.

NumPy's array-creation routines make those intentions explicit. A shape describes the arrangement; a fill value or spacing rule describes its initial contents. Our greenhouse schedule is an invented example of that distinction.

numpy-indexing.title: Working on Part of a Large Scientific Record
blocks: Scientific arrays can be too large to copy every time a calculation needs a subset. Regular stretches of storage can often be described by a starting position, a length, and a step.

NumPy distinguishes basic slicing, which can share storage, from advanced indexing, which gathers values into a new array. Those documented rules explain both the convenience of selection and the need for care when editing it.

numpy-reshaping.title: Separating Stored Order From the Shape of a Calculation
blocks: Scientific instruments and file formats often deliver observations in a flat sequence. Numerical calculations need arrangements that identify time, location, and measurement channels.

NumPy's manipulation routines describe shape and axis changes explicitly. This makes array-oriented calculations possible without treating every change of layout as a new measurement. The documented distinction between reshape, transpose, and joining is the mechanism we use here.

numpy-broadcasting.title: Repeating a Calculation Without Repeating Its Data
blocks: Array calculations often combine a large collection with a smaller reference: one scale for all entries, or one target for each feature column. Explicitly constructing a second large table adds work and obscures that the reference is shared.

NumPy's broadcasting rules specify when smaller shapes can be reused across larger ones. Our greenhouse example illustrates one such case. It is not a claim that NumPy understands the meaning of the columns; matching the references to the right columns remains our responsibility.

numpy-masks.title: Selecting Observations Without Rewriting the Table

sources.title: Python: lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries

blocks: Selecting observations is a recurring problem in scientific computing: a calculation might need only a certain period, a particular group, or measurements that satisfy a condition. Keeping a decision beside each observation separates the selection rule from the stored measurements.

NumPy documents Boolean indexing as a way to use those decisions. This lesson uses invented greenhouse readings to show the mechanism. It teaches selection, not a claim that all unusual observations should be discarded.

numpy-reductions.title: Turning a Large Report Into a Specific Answer
blocks: Scientists needed summaries long before NumPy: totals, central values, and measures of variation compress observations into answers to particular questions. Array libraries must make clear which observations each summary combines.

NumPy's statistical reductions accept axes, while functions such as argmax return positions instead of measurements. Keeping that distinction explicit lets a numerical summary remain connected to its original observation.

numpy-vectorisation.title: Moving Repeated Arithmetic Into Numerical Routines
blocks: Scientific Python programs often repeat a small arithmetic rule over many observations. Performing each iteration through Python has overhead, while compiled array routines can carry out many such operations directly.

NumPy exposes common elementwise operations as universal functions, often shortened to ufuncs. This lets us express the numerical rule at array scale. It does not eliminate the need to inspect temporary arrays or prove that the rule matches the intended calculation.

numpy-linear-algebra.title: Reusing Numerical Linear Algebra for Many Observations
blocks: Solving systems of equations and fitting more equations than there are unknowns are longstanding numerical problems. Reliable implementations need algorithms that account for rounding and the structure of the system.

NumPy's linear algebra interface draws on established BLAS and LAPACK routines. We use that interface after making the small matrix calculation visible, and distinguish solving an exact square system from fitting an overdetermined one.

numpy-numerical-checks.title: Representing Real Quantities With Finite Storage
blocks: A computer has a finite number of bits for each stored numerical value. Many decimal fractions therefore cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point storage. Repeated arithmetic must round intermediate results.

NumPy exposes data types, finite-value checks, and approximate comparisons so a program can account for those limitations. The tolerance is part of our numerical contract, not a way to declare every discrepancy harmless.

reproducible-sampling.title: Giving Simulated Experiments a Repeatable Starting Point
blocks: Numerical simulations need many values that behave like random draws, yet debugging also requires the ability to repeat an experiment. Pseudorandom generators address this by maintaining a state and updating it through a deterministic rule.

NumPy separates the bit generator from the interface that draws values. Its PCG64 documentation specifies how an initial seed establishes a stream. Our lesson uses this distinction to explain repeatability; the workshop receives already chosen indices and does not implement a random-number generator.

numpy-functions.title: Making Numerical Routines Reusable Without Losing Their Assumptions
blocks: Reusable numerical routines let programmers test one implementation and call it from many calculations. Their usefulness depends on the caller and the routine agreeing about dimensions, units, and valid inputs.

NumPy's array conversion and testing interfaces support those contracts. They let a Python function accept array-like input, validate its layout, and compare a result with a small independently checked example. The function remains responsible for its scientific assumptions.

numpy-saving-data.title: Keeping Numerical Results Usable by the Next Program
blocks: Scientific programs need to exchange data and repeat earlier calculations. Plain text is inspectable, but it does not automatically preserve every array's type, shape, labels, or full numerical precision.

NumPy's NPY format records an array's dtype and shape with its values. NPZ archives collect named arrays, while text readers and writers serve simpler interchange needs. These formats preserve stored data, not the scientific meaning we forget to record.

sql-tables.title: Queries Should Survive a Change in Storage
blocks: Programs once depended heavily on the paths used to find stored records. Codd’s 1970 relational model proposed describing data through relations so applications could depend less on its physical arrangement.

Our maintenance tables use that separation: an asset ID identifies a pump without telling us which disk page holds it. The invented records illustrate the idea; SQL tables also permit duplicates unless constraints or queries remove them.

sql-select.title: Choose a Result Without Writing a Storage Walk
blocks: Chamberlin and Boyce’s 1974 SEQUEL paper described composing operations on tables to express a query. The user specified the desired information without writing a record-navigation program.
Selecting fields and eliminating repeated result rows remain separate choices in SQL. That distinction lets the maintenance register support both an asset list and a site-category report.

sql-where.title: Describe the Condition Instead of the Search Procedure
blocks: Relational query languages made a condition on a table part of the request. SEQUEL’s composable table operations helped readers express which records they wanted while leaving the search strategy to the database.
A maintenance rule can therefore be reviewed independently of whether the engine scans rows or uses an index. The examples here use simple invented records so we can inspect each decision ourselves.

sql-order-limit.title: Storage Independence Also Removed an Accidental Order
blocks: Relational systems separate the logical result from the physical access path. System R explored how a high-level relational interface could work over changing storage choices.

The consequence for a shortlist is practical: order must be requested as part of the query. A scan order that looked stable is not a ranking rule. Our example supplies a tie breaker so the selected visits are reproducible.

sql-null.title: Database Implementations Had to Agree About Missing Values
blocks: An absent value complicates ordinary comparisons: we cannot determine whether an unknown duration equals ten. SQLite’s NULL documentation describes compatibility tests performed in 2002 to compare how other SQL engines handled these cases.
The resulting behaviours include distinctions between equality predicates, grouping and duplicate removal. We study those operations explicitly instead of treating NULL as a special number.

sql-case.title: A Query Result Can Include a Decision
blocks: SQL developed beyond selecting stored columns to include expressions that derive values inside a result. Conditional expressions let applications describe row-level decisions close to the data that determines them.
CASE does not update the sensor record. It adds a computed label to the result, which means the policy can be inspected and changed without overwriting the observed temperature.

sql-aggregates.title: A Report Needed Fewer Rows Than the Log
blocks: Database query languages had to support reports that combined many stored records into a small result. Aggregate functions make the reduction explicit so the query can state what is counted or combined.
SQLite documents its aggregate treatment of missing and empty inputs. The maintenance example uses those rules to distinguish visits that exist from durations that were actually measured.

sql-group-by.title: One Summary Was Not Enough for a Comparative Report
blocks: Reporting queries needed subtotals for departments, products and other categories rather than a single database-wide value. SQL grouping describes the shared values that define each subtotal.

The maintenance version is concrete: place every P1 visit in one collection and every P2 visit in another. Aggregate each collection independently. This is a query result grouping, not a change to how the records must be stored.

sql-having.title: Reports Needed Conditions on Subtotals
blocks: Once query languages could return grouped totals, users also needed to select groups by those totals: customers with repeated purchases, departments above a budget, or assets with recurring findings.

WHERE applies to the input rows and HAVING applies to the groups. The distinction follows the different information available at those stages. A row’s finding is known before grouping; the number of qualifying visits in its group is known after grouping.

sql-inner-joins.title: Separate Facts Could Be Recombined by Their Values
blocks: The relational model allowed related facts to live in separate relations and be combined through matching values. This reduced the need for applications to navigate a particular chain of stored records.

Our asset-to-visit match uses the asset ID on both sides. This is a teaching example of an equijoin, where the relationship is equality of the chosen keys, rather than a claim that every join uses equality.

sql-left-joins.title: A Match-Only Query Could Hide Missing Evidence
blocks: Reporting from related tables raises a second question beyond finding matches: which items have none? Outer joins extend a matching result with rows that preserve selected unmatched records.

The left side defines the population to retain. In this lesson that population is the asset register, so the absence of inspection evidence remains visible instead of removing the asset from the report.

sql-join-grain.title: Correct Matching Can Still Change What a Row Means
blocks: Relational operations compose, so a result from one operation can become the input to another. That power also makes it necessary to track the meaning and multiplicity of intermediate rows. SQL’s join semantics emit matching pairs, including every permitted combination.

A database cannot infer that a later SUM was meant to count each inspection only once. Our repair explicitly produces asset-level summaries before joining them. This follows from the required report grain rather than a special rule about maintenance data.

sql-subqueries.title: A Query Could Supply Another Query’s Input
blocks: Once a question depends on a quantity calculated from stored records, a query language needs a way to compose those operations. SQL subqueries put a SELECT inside another statement. Modern SQLite and PostgreSQL document both independent subqueries and correlated ones whose values depend on an outer row.

Our inspection average is a small example of that composition. It keeps the calculation with the comparison, while leaving us responsible for the shape of the inner result and the meaning of missing values.

sql-exists.title: Finding Absence Without Manufacturing More Rows

sources.title: PostgreSQL EXISTS and NOT IN semantics

blocks: Relational queries often need to express that a related fact is present or absent. SQL’s EXISTS expression answers that question from the presence of rows, while NOT EXISTS reverses it. This keeps the result at the outer table’s grain instead of producing one row for every matching pair.
The distinction is useful for a maintenance log that can contain several visits per pump. We care whether any completed visit exists, not how many matching copies a join could produce.

sql-set-operations.title: Combining Results Needed a Duplicate Policy
blocks: SQL result combinations draw on set operations, but ordinary query results may contain repeated rows. SQL therefore distinguishes UNION, which removes duplicate result rows, from UNION ALL, which retains them. INTERSECT and EXCEPT describe common rows and rows left after subtraction.

That choice matters at the maintenance desk. Repeated alerts can be useful events in one report and unwanted repeated pump assignments in another. We need to choose the result’s meaning before deciding whether two equal rows should collapse.

sql-ctes.title: Names Made Intermediate Relations Easier to Review
blocks: Nested queries let one operation use another’s result, but deeply nested expressions can be awkward to inspect. Common table expressions give those intermediate relations names inside one statement. SQLite added CTE support in its February 2014 release.

This is a language feature for expressing dependencies. Naming closed_jobs does not permanently create a table or promise a particular execution strategy. Its value for our report is that the next stage clearly receives completed work rather than every job in the system.

sql-recursive-ctes.title: Repeated Relationships Needed More Than a Fixed Join

sources.title: SQLite WITH and recursive query examples
PostgreSQL recursive queries and cycle detection

blocks: A parts list, reporting hierarchy or network can contain an unknown number of levels. Recursive CTEs let a query start from a known row and repeatedly follow a relationship. The database documents describe that repeated expansion explicitly, including examples where a cycle would otherwise keep producing work.

The maintenance question is the same one: which records can we reach from this starting point? Our path guard rejects a return to a node already on the current path. A separate depth limit bounds how far this particular report is allowed to explore.

sql-window-functions.title: Analytical Queries Needed to Keep Their Detail
blocks: Ordinary aggregation answers questions about groups by producing fewer rows. Analytical reports often need a group calculation beside the original rows instead. Window functions provide that arrangement. SQLite added window-function support in September 2018.

For the technician, this means a reading can retain its timestamp and identity while receiving a position within its pump’s history. That position is meaningful only after we define the partition and its ordering.

sql-window-frames.title: An Ordered Group Still Needed a Boundary
blocks: Adding an order to an analytical calculation makes questions such as “so far” possible, but it leaves another choice: how many neighbouring rows should contribute? Window frames make that boundary part of the query. Default frame rules can include all peers sharing the current ordering value.

That explains our apparent jump. If timestamp alone defines peers, both records at that timestamp can enter a cumulative frame together. A physical-row frame and a complete ordering express a different, equally deliberate calculation.

sql-dates.title: Event Logs and Calendars Answer Different Questions
blocks: Time values have to represent both instants and calendar conventions. SQLite supports date calculations over defined text and numeric representations rather than a dedicated date/time storage type. That makes a consistent representation an application responsibility.

A daily report needs more than a timestamp function. It needs a set of expected days. Joining a calendar to an event log preserves days that have no matching event, just as an asset register preserves pumps that have no visit.

sql-text.title: Matching Text Required Rules Beyond Its Appearance
blocks: Text processing in SQL includes both exact comparisons and pattern matching. Those operations developed different conventions: a pattern can reserve characters to stand for something else, while comparison rules decide which text values count as equal.

For imported identifiers, the useful lesson is to name the convention. We use ordinary surrounding spaces, ASCII letter case and a literal underscore. That limited rule is easy to demonstrate and test without pretending it solves every language’s text behaviour.

sql-json.title: Structured Messages Entered Relational Queries

sources.title: SQLite JSON functions and their inclusion since 3.38.0

blocks: Services commonly exchange structured messages as JSON, while analysis often happens in relational tables. Database JSON functions let queries inspect those messages without first flattening every property into a permanent column. SQLite made its JSON functions built in by default in version 3.38.0 in February 2022.

That convenience does not erase the payload’s types. A numeric property, a text property and an absent property still mean different things. Our report uses that distinction before it allows a value into a temperature calculation.

sql-feature-tables.title: Training Data Needed a Memory of What Was Available

sources.title: Feast point-in-time joins and created-timestamp filtering

blocks: Feature-store systems address the problem of joining historical features to the time of each training example. Feast documents point-in-time retrieval relative to each entity timestamp, including a bounded lookback. Its current documentation also distinguishes event time from when a value became available.

That distinction explains our late upload. Filtering event time alone cannot exclude data that arrived after the decision. This lesson expresses both boundaries directly in SQL so their meaning remains visible regardless of the feature-store framework used later.

sql-schema-design.title: Keeping the Meaning of a Record Separate from Its Storage
blocks: Codd’s 1970 paper argued for a relational description of data that did not make users depend on physical storage arrangements. A logical table needs a stable interpretation even when the database changes how it stores its rows. Our equipment register uses that distinction: an asset identity should survive a new sort order or index.

SQLite later made a deliberate choice to support flexible value typing. Its STRICT table option, introduced in version 3.37.0 in 2021, provides stronger type enforcement for applications that want it. The browser exercises use SQLite 3.39-compatible syntax and make those dialect choices explicit.

sql-constraints.title: Preserving Relationships Across Several Writers
blocks: Relational tables let records be connected through values instead of application-specific pointers. That independence makes relationship rules important: any writer can otherwise introduce a child record whose parent is absent. Foreign keys put that relationship check in the database.

SQLite’s documentation records foreign-key enforcement beginning in version 3.6.19 in 2009. It must be enabled for each connection in the configuration used here. The browser runner enables it before executing your statements. Merely seeing REFERENCES in a schema is insufficient evidence that a particular connection enforces it.

sql-normalization.title: Reducing Facts That Have to Be Updated Together
blocks: Relational design made it possible to describe data independently of a file’s arrangement. It also raised a design problem: several table layouts can represent the same apparent facts while behaving differently under updates. Work on dependencies and normal forms addressed those redundancies.

Our repeated pump-site example shows an update anomaly directly. Splitting the records helps only if the decomposition preserves the facts and supports the rules the application must enforce. A smaller table is not automatically a better design.

sql-insert-update-delete.title: Describing a Set of Rows to Change
blocks: The early SEQUEL work described composable operations over tabular data. That set-oriented approach also means an update can target many records at once. The useful question becomes which rows satisfy the write’s predicate.

Modern dialects add ways to handle duplicate identities during insertion. SQLite’s UPSERT follows PostgreSQL-style ON CONFLICT syntax, with its own details. Our revision rule is an application policy layered on that mechanism; the database does not know which imported status is newer unless we specify it.

sql-transactions.title: Making a Business Operation Survive a Failure
blocks: Transaction-processing research addressed operations whose meaning spanned several low-level writes. Jim Gray’s 1981 paper described the transaction concept and its limitations. The problem was practical: interruptions should not leave half of an intended database operation visible as a completed result.

Our spare-parts transfer is an invented example of that boundary. It updates database records only. Sending a delivery truck or an email involves another system whose effects are not automatically reversed by a SQL rollback.

sql-concurrency.title: Coordinating Readers and Writers Without Losing Work
blocks: Shared databases needed to coordinate transactions whose operations overlapped. Locking and multi-version approaches provide different ways to control which state a transaction can observe and change. These mechanisms developed to support concurrent applications, long before a model could issue SQL.

SQLite and PostgreSQL expose different concurrency models. SQLite serialises writers, while WAL mode lets readers keep an earlier snapshot as a writer commits. PostgreSQL offers several isolation levels with their own anomaly and retry rules. Our one-connection exercise illustrates an optimistic version predicate, not either engine’s full scheduler.

sql-indexes.title: Letting the Database Choose an Access Path

sources.title: Selinger and colleagues: Access path selection, 1979

blocks: SQL lets a caller describe desired records without specifying their physical traversal. System R’s 1979 access-path paper described choosing routes for queries, including joins. Indexes provide candidate routes that the optimiser can compare with reading a table.

Our pump-and-time example gives a physical intuition: equal leading keys occupy a region of an ordered index. The widget lays out records directly; it does not implement database pages, B-tree balancing or disk I/O.

sql-query-plans.title: Choosing Work from a Declarative Request
blocks: The System R work showed how a database could choose access paths for a declarative request instead of requiring the caller to prescribe every step. That freedom creates several possible plans for the same logical result. Estimating their costs depends on what the engine knows about the data.

EXPLAIN facilities make some of those choices visible. Their formats and meanings are engine-specific, and SQLite warns that its query-plan output can change. We will inspect plan structure without treating exact display text as an application API.

sql-parameters-permissions.title: Separating Query Structure from Supplied Data
blocks: Database applications needed to reuse a query while supplying different values. Driver parameter interfaces separate those values from SQL structure. That same boundary prevents a value containing SQL punctuation from being reinterpreted as part of the query when used correctly.

Database access control developed alongside shared data systems because syntactically valid queries can still access the wrong records. Parameter binding and authorisation solve different problems. Botie’s maintenance search needs both, even though our isolated browser database has no production users or server roles.

sql-data-quality.title: Checking the Facts Before Combining Them

sources.title: TensorFlow Data Validation: Detecting schema and distribution problems

blocks: Relational constraints supplied ways to keep declared identities and relationships consistent. Analytical pipelines also receive raw data that must be inspected before it is admitted to those curated tables. A staging area makes it possible to report failed records rather than losing the evidence at the first rejected insert.

Machine-learning data tools later added schema and distribution comparisons to that practice. Our SQL audit addresses selected deterministic rules for invented sensor records. It cannot establish that labels are correct or that a dataset represents the population a model will encounter.

sql-incremental-pipelines.title: Remembering a Change Position Instead of Recopying Everything
blocks: Databases maintain change information to recover and coordinate writes. Change-data-capture systems can expose committed changes to downstream consumers instead of forcing every consumer to recopy the full source. PostgreSQL logical decoding is one documented implementation with its own restart, retention and delivery responsibilities.

A consumer still needs a recoverable position and a replay policy. Our source supplies a strictly increasing ingestion sequence and per-record versions. These are explicit teaching contracts; an arbitrary timestamp column does not automatically provide the same guarantees.

nosql-data-models.title: A Shopping Cart Had to Survive a Busy Service
blocks: Amazon’s 2007 Dynamo paper describes services such as shopping carts that needed highly available reads and writes. Its interface retrieved an object by a key. Concentrating on that access pattern let the designers make different tradeoffs from a system intended to answer arbitrary relational queries. Dynamo is a particular distributed design; its choices do not define every database called NoSQL.

Our invented maintenance service is much smaller, but we can ask the same first question: what operation must remain practical? The pump screen supplies an asset ID and wants its visits. Grouping visits under that identity makes the requested association visible. We still have to decide how writes keep the grouping current.

nosql-key-value.title: Small Operations Around Explicit Keys
blocks: Redis began in 2009 under Salvatore Sanfilippo. Its string commands illustrate a small interaction: set a value under a key, then retrieve that key. A server can implement that interface without interpreting the application meaning of a pump name.

That division gives the application responsibility for a naming convention. Our site and asset pair is an invented example. The key must carry enough identity before a key-value service can return the intended record.

nosql-cache-expiry.title: A Helpful Copy Can Become a Dependency

sources.title: AWS Builders’ Library: caching challenges and strategies

blocks: Amazon’s published caching experience describes a recurring operational problem: a service becomes accustomed to the reduced source load of a warm cache, then a cold or unavailable cache exposes the source to many more requests. Caching changes the operating conditions of the service.

Redis makes expiry an explicit property of a key. A timeout gives a copy a limited lifetime; the application still chooses a lifetime appropriate to its data. Our workshop isolates the decision at that boundary. It cannot establish whether a source can absorb refresh traffic.

nosql-documents.title: Keeping Object Structure in the Stored Record
blocks: MongoDB’s April 2010 manual already describes JSON-style objects and BSON storage. This offered applications a way to retain nested fields instead of flattening every object into one row shape. The historical manual records that design; it is not a claim that MongoDB invented structured records.

For our maintenance screen, a sensor object keeps a reading beside its unit. The remaining question is whether every writer supplies the fields the reader expects. Flexible document shapes make a shared contract more useful, not less necessary.

nosql-embedding-references.title: A Document Boundary Also Became an Update Boundary
blocks: MongoDB’s early manual described embedded objects and references resolved through additional reads. The document model made locality a modelling decision: related information could travel together, while independently maintained objects could keep their own identities.

The maintenance example puts that decision under pressure. A pump’s installed sensor configuration belongs with the pump. A supplier’s current phone number is shared. A purchase-time supplier name may be a historical snapshot that should remain unchanged. Their relationships look similar on a screen but require different update rules.

nosql-document-queries.title: Queries Followed Fields Inside the Document
blocks: The early MongoDB manual describes reaching into objects through field paths. That let applications ask about nested content rather than fetching every document by ID and inspecting it themselves. Arrays introduced another question: which member must satisfy a combination of conditions?

MongoDB’s $elemMatch expresses that at least one array member must satisfy all of its listed criteria. Our workshop makes the same binding visible by expanding each reading with its parent identity, applying both conditions to that row, and then returning each matching asset once.

nosql-document-updates.title: Updating an Object Required More Than Replacing Its Copy
blocks: MongoDB’s early interface included field-level update operators as well as document replacement. That distinction let a caller change a specified part of an object without resending every field. It addressed the practical difference between altering a value and replacing an entire stored record.

Current MongoDB documentation describes atomic single-document writes and recommends including an expected current value in a write filter when concurrent updates must be coordinated. Our version check is a teaching example of that condition. The Python function exposes the rule but does not implement concurrent database access.

nosql-document-indexes.title: Document Queries Still Needed Access Paths
blocks: MongoDB’s early documentation included indexes alongside document queries. Storing a flexible object did not remove the older database problem of finding a small result without scanning every stored record. A secondary structure could organise selected field values for repeated reads.

Our teaching index groups documents by site. It exposes candidate reduction without claiming to reproduce MongoDB’s B-tree implementation or planner. We then examine a real compound index as a server-side way to support the site and temperature conditions together.

nosql-aggregation-pipelines.title: Document Applications Needed Reporting Operations Too
blocks: MongoDB’s August 2012 release announcement introduced its aggregation framework for reporting and analysis over stored documents. Applications needed more than retrieving one object: they needed to select records, reshape them and combine values into reports.

A pipeline expresses those changes as ordered stages. That makes our maintenance report readable as a sequence of record transformations. It also makes a mistake inspectable: after expanding an array, the rows represent visits, so repeating a pump-level quantity on each row can inflate a later sum.

nosql-partition-keys.title: Distributing Work Without Losing the Lookup Address

sources.title: Dynamo: Amazon’s highly available key-value store (2007)

blocks: The 2007 Dynamo paper described a key-value service designed around availability requirements at Amazon. Partitioning assigned parts of the key space to storage nodes so growth did not require every node to hold every primary record. Its hashing and replication design are a documented historical example, not the algorithm implemented by our widget.

The useful intuition is an address: a request carries a key that tells the system where to look. Requests with the same address still converge on the same logical item or grouping. A large number of possible keys does not help if almost every request uses one of them.

nosql-wide-column.title: Keeping Nearby Records Together for a Known Query

sources.title: Bigtable: A distributed storage system for structured data (2006)

blocks: Google’s 2006 Bigtable paper described a sorted map for large structured datasets, with rows, column families and timestamped values. Cassandra later combined ideas from systems including Bigtable and Dynamo, while developing its own storage and consistency behaviour. These names do not identify one interchangeable database model.

For our maintenance example, locality is the useful idea: store the records needed by one bounded query together, and order them by the field the query ranges over. Cassandra’s partition and clustering columns express those different jobs explicitly.

nosql-replication-consistency.title: Keeping a Service Usable When Copies Cannot Communicate

sources.title: Dynamo: Amazon’s highly available key-value store (2007)
Gilbert and Lynch: Perspectives on the CAP theorem

blocks: Dynamo made explicit choices about accepting operations and reconciling versions when replicas were unavailable. Gilbert and Lynch’s work on CAP explains why a replicated read/write service cannot guarantee both linearizable responses and a response to every request at a non-failing node under an arbitrary network partition.

A disconnected replica cannot discover which remote write completed. Returning its local value can preserve a response while violating the stronger read contract. Waiting or rejecting the operation preserves that contract at the expense of CAP availability for that request. This is a failure-time constraint, not a rule that every database must always choose two letters.

nosql-conditional-writes.title: Testing the Precondition at the Write Boundary
blocks: A read followed by an unconditional write leaves a gap in which another writer can change the record. Conditional updates address that gap by making the check part of the write operation. DynamoDB condition expressions and MongoDB update filters are concrete database interfaces for this idea.

This is the same concurrency problem encountered in the SQL versioned update. The syntax changes, while the reasoning stays useful: the application states which existing state would make its proposed action valid, and the database checks that condition atomically within the operation’s supported scope.

nosql-conflicts.title: Choosing Merge Rules That Fit the Operation

sources.title: Dynamo: Amazon’s highly available key-value store (2007)
Preguiça, Baquero and Shapiro: Conflict-free replicated data types (2018)

blocks: Dynamo described preserving divergent object versions so application logic could reconcile them. Later conflict-free replicated data type research examined data structures with precisely defined merge rules that converge under stated delivery assumptions. Redis Active-Active is one product family that uses CRDT ideas; this does not mean every Redis deployment has those semantics.

Our counter is a teaching instance of a state-based grow-only counter. We derive its merge from ownership and monotonic updates. It is suitable for accumulated inspections under those assumptions, not for every mutable document or bounded stock balance.

nosql-streams-projections.title: Letting a Committed Change Feed Another Read View
blocks: Database logs and change notifications allow downstream systems to follow committed changes instead of repeatedly scanning a source for differences. DynamoDB Streams and MongoDB change streams expose such changes through different APIs and retention contracts. They are examples of the mechanism, not interchangeable delivery protocols.

A stream can close the application’s source-write/notification gap when its guarantees match the design. It still leaves the consumer responsible for applying changes, recovering its position and handling its own side effects. Our local projection focuses on those applied-state semantics.

nosql-schema-evolution.title: Letting Old and New Records Coexist During a Change
blocks: Document databases permit records with different shapes, which can make a gradual rollout possible. MongoDB’s schema-versioning pattern documents an explicit version field and readers that understand the relevant shapes. The ability to store both versions is a mechanism; compatibility still has to be implemented.

The maintenance problem is a units change as well as a field move. An adapter can connect both representations to the same interpreted measurement while keeping their original meaning visible. Guessing from whichever field happens to exist would hide malformed or future records.

nosql-recovery.title: Retaining an Earlier State After the Current Copies Change

sources.title: DynamoDB restore to a new table

blocks: Database backup mechanisms preserve earlier data so operational mistakes and storage failures need not destroy the only recoverable state. Different products expose different units: Cassandra documents snapshots and incremental backups; DynamoDB provides managed backup and point-in-time restore mechanisms. Neither is reproduced by our local dictionary.

The useful recovery idea is a boundary. A snapshot establishes a known earlier state; a valid replay interval brings that state to a chosen later point. The target must fall inside the history the backup system can actually recover.

nosql-ml-records.title: Separating Fast Current Lookups from Reproducible Training History
blocks: Feature-store systems separate concerns that otherwise get mixed into one table: serving inputs quickly by entity and retaining information for training or analysis. SageMaker documents online and offline storage modes with distinct update and history behaviour. They are one implementation of this separation, not a requirement that every model use a specialised store.

Our maintenance system already has historical SQL feature logic. Here we decide what a current serving lookup must return and which checks belong between that lookup and the model. The storage format is useful only if it preserves the feature contract.

graph-database-models.title: Relationships Became Part of the Stored Model

sources.title: Cypher authors on the historical data-model problem

blocks: The Cypher authors describe Neo4j’s early data-model work in a media asset management system around 2000. Its changing structures, relationships and access-control views made variable-length connection queries useful. This is one documented route into modern property graphs, rather than a claim that Neo4j invented graphs. A property graph gives entities nodes and stores typed relationships with properties of their own.

This changes how we express a dependency question. The relationship is a stored fact we can follow from a known starting asset. It does not make every query faster, and relational tables can represent the same facts with keys and joins.

graph-database-identity.title: A Graph Needed Stable References Beyond Display Names

sources.title: RDF identity and shared resource descriptions, W3C 1999

blocks: Sharing descriptions between systems made identity a practical problem for early web metadata. W3C’s 1999 RDF recommendation addressed exchangeable resource descriptions, where common references matter more than a displayed name. Our property-graph import has a related problem at a smaller scale: local pump IDs need enough scope to refer to the intended entity. The mechanisms differ, but neither model can safely equate entities from matching display text alone.

A source-qualified equipment code makes the scope visible. It prevents an import from treating identical local names as global identifiers, while allowing a later display-name change on the same entity.

graph-pattern-matching.title: A Query Could Describe the Connected Shape It Wanted

sources.title: Francis and colleagues, Cypher language paper, 2018

blocks: Cypher developed inside Neo4j as a declarative property-graph language. Its 2018 language paper explains pattern matching as producing rows of variable bindings: each row records which entities satisfy a connected pattern.

That is why the inspection variable matters. Once a row binds it to I1, the technician relationship must extend from I1. The drawing-like syntax makes this connection visible while leaving physical execution to the database.

graph-filtering-aggregation.title: Graph Matches Still Produce Rows That Need a Grain
blocks: Pattern matching can produce many binding rows from one starting node. Cypher combines those rows using aggregate functions and explicit intermediate stages such as WITH. The result depends on what is counted and which bindings remain as grouping keys.

Our duplicate link shows the practical consequence. The graph can contain two matched relationships while representing one inspection entity. Counting the entity once requires an identity-based duplicate policy.

graph-optional-patterns.title: Absence Became a Result Worth Preserving
blocks: Cypher OPTIONAL MATCH extends pattern matching with NULL bindings when the requested pattern has no match. This resembles an outer join: existing input rows can survive without a related record.
That behaviour lets an asset register define the report population. A missing completed inspection is then visible as absence, instead of causing the asset itself to disappear.

graph-traversal-cycles.title: Unknown-Length Connections Needed Repeated Expansion

sources.title: Cypher authors on variable-length traversal needs

blocks: The early Neo4j use case described by the Cypher authors included access through variable-length relationships. A fixed sequence of joins or pattern segments cannot express every unknown chain length conveniently. Graph query languages therefore provide bounded or variable-length path matching.

The repeated step does not decide the answer’s grain. A list of reachable nodes, every distinct path and the shortest path are different questions. Our teaching traversal collects nodes once, which gives the visited set a clear purpose.

graph-shortest-paths.title: Shortest Routes Needed a Cost-Aware Search

sources.title: Dijkstra, A note on two problems in connexion with graphs, 1959

blocks: Dijkstra’s 1959 paper described a procedure for finding the shortest route between nodes in a weighted graph. The useful step is to separate tentative distances from settled ones: with nonnegative lengths, the least tentative distance cannot later be improved by taking a detour through a more expensive unsettled node.

Dijkstra’s shortest-path method is used to find minimum accumulated cost in graphs with suitable nonnegative weights. Neo4j’s Graph Data Science documentation exposes that method separately from simple hop-count path matching. The algorithm keeps the cheapest unsettled distance visible rather than committing to the first route discovered.

For our cart, that distinction allows a route with an extra stop to win. The Python exercise implements a small nonnegative-weight version so we can inspect why the earlier expensive route is replaced.

graph-constraints-indexes.title: Flexible Records Still Needed Shared Invariants

sources.title: Neo4j constraint creation and backing indexes

blocks: Property graphs let applications evolve node properties without requiring every category to have an identical record shape. As those graphs became application databases, shared write rules remained necessary. The Cypher language paper includes schema-definition capabilities alongside queries and updates; current Neo4j constraints make selected identity and property requirements enforceable.

The purpose here is narrower than making every node identical. All Asset nodes need an unambiguous application identity, while different kinds of equipment can still have different optional properties.

graph-safe-updates.title: Connected Updates Needed a Transaction Boundary
blocks: A graph update can change an entity and several attached relationships together. Transaction support provides a boundary within which the database either commits the unit of work or rolls it back. Modern Neo4j drivers also retry selected transient failures, which makes the behaviour of the transaction function part of the application’s correctness.

The maintenance approval adds another boundary: a person approves a particular action against particular evidence. Rechecking that evidence at commit time prevents an old approval from silently becoming authority for a materially different state.

graph-imports.title: Bulk Data Exchange Had to Survive Partial Progress
blocks: Graph loaders need to resolve source identities to stored nodes before creating their relationships. Neo4j’s documented import workflows combine row-oriented input with matching and merge operations, while transaction batching changes the unit of rollback.

The operational problem is older than any one loader: a response can be lost after work commits. Stable source identities and a recorded checkpoint make replay a question of recognising prior work rather than assuming every arrival is new.

graph-query-performance.title: Declarative Graph Queries Needed Physical Execution Plans
blocks: A declarative pattern describes the answer, leaving the database to choose how to find it. The Cypher authors describe Neo4j’s cost-based planning and physical execution operators. This separation lets equivalent logical queries use different access paths.

For our maintenance graph, locating one asset before expanding relationships can avoid unrelated work. The improvement is a claim to verify in a real plan, because cardinality estimates, indexes and graph degree all affect execution.

graph-rdf-sparql.title: Web Resources Needed Descriptions That Could Travel
blocks: W3C’s 1999 RDF recommendation addressed machine-readable descriptions of Web resources. Shared identifiers and statement structure let descriptions from different applications be combined without agreeing on one table layout. The later RDF 1.1 and SPARQL 1.1 recommendations specify the graph model and its query language.

That helps our two maintenance teams state which resource a claim concerns. Agreement on identifiers and predicates still requires modelling work. Publishing a statement in RDF does not establish that it is correct.

graph-provenance.title: Derived Results Needed a Traceable History
blocks: W3C’s 2013 PROV recommendations gave applications a shared way to describe the entities and activities involved in producing information, including who was responsible. A chart could be linked to the dataset and transformation that produced it rather than circulating without that history.

Our maintenance claims have the same need on a smaller scale. A recorded source helps us inspect a disagreement or withdraw a superseded claim. Provenance explains how information arrived; it is not a certificate of truth.

graph-ml-retrieval.title: Some Questions Needed Connections Across Retrieved Passages
blocks: The 2024 GraphRAG paper studied questions that require a broad view of a document collection. Its method builds an entity graph and community summaries to support query-focused summarisation. It addresses a different failure from simply finding a nearby text passage.

Our maintenance example uses a smaller local retrieval mechanism: start from a known asset and follow approved dependency types to related manuals. It is not a reproduction of that paper’s community-summary pipeline. The common motivation is that useful evidence may be connected across records.

missing-measurements.title: The Missing Observation Has a Story Too
blocks: Incomplete records posed a problem for statistical inference long before modern neural networks. Ignoring an absent observation can change the group we describe, especially when absence is related to the value we wanted to measure.

Rubin's 1976 paper established conditions under which the missingness process can be ignored for particular forms of inference. It did not say that replacing every blank with an average is universally valid. Our invented greenhouse example uses mean replacement as a transparent baseline so we can inspect exactly what it assumes.

categorical-encoding.title: Giving Each Category Its Own Question
blocks: Statistical models need representations for properties that are names rather than quantities. Indicator variables answer separate membership questions, allowing categories to contribute without forcing their arbitrary codes onto a numerical scale.

Modern preprocessing libraries document one-hot encoding as one way to create those indicators. Our roof materials are an invented example. The practical contribution we need is the representation: one fixed column per known category, with a clear policy for unfamiliar categories.

cyclical-features.title: Representing a Repeating Cycle as a Position
blocks: Time-related measurements create a practical modelling problem: day, week, and seasonal cycles have boundaries in their written numbering that are not boundaries in the phenomenon. A representation that ignores repetition can make neighbouring times look unrelated.

Sine and cosine coordinates use the familiar geometry of a circle to preserve a cycle's continuity. Scikit-learn's time-feature example documents this representation among several modelling choices. Our greenhouse clock is an invented teaching example, and we are not presenting the circle representation as a newly invented algorithm.

record-quality.title: Why a Dataset Needs Its Own Instructions

sources.title: Gebru and colleagues: Datasheets for Datasets

blocks: A dataset can outlive the people who remember how it was collected. When collection details disappear, later users may mistake a convenient table for a complete description of a population.

Gebru and colleagues introduced datasheets for datasets in 2018, with a later journal publication, to document matters such as motivation, composition, collection, and recommended uses. Our duplicate-log exercise handles one small part of that broader problem: recording what an observation means before deciding how to clean it.

data-leakage.title: When a Successful Evaluation Used Unavailable Information

sources.title: Kaufman and colleagues: Leakage in Data Mining (2012)
Scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and data leakage

blocks: When we combine records from several systems, a later event can slip into the inputs for an earlier prediction. Preprocessing can also use information from data we intended to hold out. The resulting score then reflects information the model would not have had when it needed to make the real decision.

Kaufman and colleagues examined leakage as information about a target that is not legitimately available to the prediction process. Our invented repair records make the timing issue explicit. Other forms include fitting preprocessing on test data or placing copies of an observation on both sides of a split.

class-imbalance.title: Learning From a Class That Appears Only Occasionally
blocks: Consider a classifier trained on records where one outcome is much more common than the other. It can reduce its total mistakes by favouring the common class, even if the rare cases are the ones we most need to find. Work on imbalanced classification addresses that mismatch between a convenient training objective and the job the model is meant to do.

Chawla and colleagues' 2002 SMOTE paper studied synthetic minority oversampling, creating additional minority examples between nearby observations. That is one response to imbalance, not a universal remedy. Our lesson first makes the evaluation problem visible; it does not generate synthetic sensor records.

baseline-predictions.title: A Prediction Needs a Reference for Comparison
blocks: Predictive modelling needs control comparisons. Without them, a score cannot show whether a method gained anything from its inputs beyond a simple summary of previous outcomes.

Modern evaluation libraries preserve this practice through baseline estimators that ignore input features and predict a training summary. This is not an invention claim for one library. Our invented greenhouse example uses the training mean to make the comparison explicit before introducing more capable predictors.

learning-curves.title: Model Comparisons Depend on How Much Data We Have

sources.title: Perlich, Provost, and Simonoff: A Learning-Curve Analysis (2003)

blocks: A comparison at one dataset size can hide how two learning methods respond as more examples become available. A method that works well with few observations need not remain the best choice with many.

Perlich, Provost, and Simonoff's 2003 study compared tree induction and logistic regression through learning curves. Our supplied greenhouse errors are invented illustrations, not results from that study or a model trained in this widget. They let us inspect the interpretation before running larger fitting experiments.

decision-thresholds.title: Separating Statistical Evidence From a Decision
blocks: Prediction systems have long needed a second step between estimating an outcome and choosing an action. The same estimated risk can justify different actions when their consequences differ.

Current threshold-tuning documentation makes that separation explicit: estimating scores and selecting a cutoff are distinct tasks. Our invented sensor costs show one simple expected-cost rule. They are teaching units, not an estimate of real maintenance costs or a recommendation for an operational safety system.

probability-calibration.title: A Correct Choice Can Still Come With Misleading Confidence

sources.title: Guo and colleagues: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks (2017)

blocks: As classifiers improved, a separate question remained: did the number attached to a prediction accurately describe its uncertainty? A model could choose the right class often while being too confident about individual choices.

Guo and colleagues' 2017 study examined this issue in modern neural networks and evaluated calibration methods, including temperature scaling. Our invented sensor group teaches how to inspect reliability before attempting a correction. It does not reproduce their experiments or establish that one adjustment works for every model.

grouped-validation.title: Repeated Measurements Need a Different Evaluation Boundary
blocks: Repeated observations are common in scientific datasets. Measurements from one person, device, or location can share properties that distinguish them from other groups. Treating all rows as independent can therefore overstate performance on new groups.

Grouped validation procedures address the evaluation boundary by keeping a group's observations together. Scikit-learn documents these splitters separately from ordinary random splits. Our invented greenhouses make the group identity visible without claiming that one split design is appropriate for every prediction task.

distribution-shift.title: When Training and Use No Longer Share the Same Distribution

sources.title: Lipton, Wang, and Smola: Detecting and Correcting for Label Shift (2018)

blocks: A predictor's evaluation can stop describing its environment when the frequencies or relationships in incoming data change. Detecting that mismatch is a separate problem from fitting the original predictor.

Lipton, Wang, and Smola's 2018 work studies label shift, where class proportions change under specific assumptions, and methods for detecting and correcting it. Our roof-category comparison is a simpler input-distribution audit. It is not their correction algorithm and does not assume that every observed change is label shift.

bootstrap-uncertainty.title: Using Computation to Recreate the Act of Sampling

sources.title: Efron: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife (1979)

blocks: Statisticians often need the uncertainty of an estimate even when a convenient formula is unavailable. Repeating the entire real-world data collection may be impractical.

Efron's 1979 bootstrap paper developed a computational approach based on resampling the observed data. Our invented greenhouse readings show how replacement and repeated estimates work. Three displayed resamples make the mechanism inspectable; they are far too few to justify a useful confidence interval.

model-residual-analysis.title: Checking What a Fitted Equation Left Behind

sources.title: NIST: Are the model residuals well-behaved?

blocks: Fitting a regression equation leaves a difference at each observation. Statistical model checking examines those differences because a fitted average can conceal a systematic pattern. The NIST engineering handbook documents checks involving residual plots and model assumptions.

Our greenhouse readings are invented. We use the same diagnostic idea: keep the part the prediction failed to explain, then ask whether it changes with temperature, time or another recorded condition.

model-precision-recall.title: Finding Relevant Items in a Much Larger Collection
blocks: Precision and recall are established measures in information retrieval: returning many documents is only useful if the relevant ones are among them, and a short clean list can still omit most relevant documents. The same counting problem appears in a rare-fault detector.
Modern classification libraries expose these measures over many score thresholds. Our pump example keeps the underlying counts visible so a curve cannot hide the inspection workload.

model-evaluation-slices.title: A Model Report Needs to Say Who Was Measured

sources.title: Mitchell and colleagues: Model Cards for Model Reporting, 2019

blocks: A single reported score can hide differences across populations and operating conditions. Model Cards proposed structured documentation of intended uses, evaluation conditions and disaggregated performance. That documented reporting proposal helps us ask where a model’s evidence actually applies.
We will use shifts in an invented greenhouse. The calculation is small enough to inspect, while the reporting question also applies to devices, locations and carefully defined population groups.

model-paired-comparisons.title: Preserving the Comparison When We Resample

sources.title: Cawley and Talbot: selection bias in performance evaluation, 2010

blocks: Comparing learning procedures requires separating a method change from variation in the evaluation data. Cawley and Talbot examined how selection itself can overfit an estimated performance criterion. A favourable comparison becomes harder to interpret when it was selected from many attempts.

Here we begin with a simpler fixed comparison. Both frozen models see the same cases. We keep each pair together when resampling so the uncertainty calculation still describes their difference on shared observations.

model-nested-validation.title: The Search Can Overfit Too

sources.title: Cawley and Talbot: On Over-fitting in Model Selection, 2010

blocks: Model fitting was already understood as a source of overfitting, but the criterion used to choose a fitted model also varies with the sample. Cawley and Talbot examined how optimising that noisy criterion can bias the reported result.
Nested cross-validation separates the search from an outer assessment. The outside observations ask whether the entire inner choosing procedure produces useful predictions on data it did not use.

model-data-audits.title: Looking for Problems in the Labels

sources.title: Northcutt, Jiang and Chuang: Confident Learning

blocks: Datasets are often treated as a fixed answer key even though their labels may contain mistakes. Confident Learning developed methods for estimating label uncertainty and identifying likely label issues using predicted probabilities under stated assumptions.

Our review queue is a simpler teaching rule, not an implementation of Confident Learning. It flags strong disagreements for investigation. The original observation and an independent review remain the evidence for any correction.

model-selective-prediction.title: Allowing a Classifier to Decline a Decision

sources.title: Geifman and El-Yaniv: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks, 2017

blocks: Selective classification studies predictions with a reject option: the system can decline some cases and trade coverage for lower error on accepted cases. Geifman and El-Yaniv developed a method for deep networks with risk control under their stated procedure.

Our threshold exercise measures empirical coverage and error on supplied cases. It does not implement that paper’s guarantee. The useful intuition is that refusing a case changes the population whose errors we report.

model-behaviour-tests.title: Testing Behaviour That a Single Score Misses

sources.title: Ribeiro and colleagues: Beyond Accuracy, CheckList, 2020

blocks: A held-out average can miss a specific behaviour that users rely on. CheckList applied behavioural testing ideas to language models, including tests of capabilities and expected responses to input changes.

We use that testing perspective for a temperature service. Our unit and batching checks are examples of declared relationships between inputs and outputs, not a claim to implement the CheckList software or certify robustness.

model-iteration-project.title: A Fitted Equation Needs an Evaluation Record

sources.title: Mitchell and colleagues: Model Cards for Model Reporting

blocks: Least-squares fitting provides coefficients that minimise squared training discrepancies for a specified linear model. It does not decide whether the inputs are appropriate or whether a revised model is useful for its intended population.

This project brings fitting together with explicit evaluation and reporting. The greenhouse is invented, and the small exact training relation makes the mechanics visible. We still keep the distinction between fitting a relation and collecting enough evidence to use it.

conditional-probability.title: Working Back From What We Observed

sources.title: Bayes, communicated by Price: An Essay Towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763)

blocks: Calculating what might happen under a known rule is one problem. Inferring something about that rule after seeing outcomes is another. Bayes's essay, communicated by Richard Price in 1763 after Bayes's death, addressed this reverse direction: what repeated successes and failures could tell us about an unknown chance.

Our alarm example is invented and uses a simpler finite table. Its useful connection to that history is the direction of reasoning. We observe the alarm, then update how plausible each possible cause is. We must account for both how well a cause explains the alarm and how common that cause was to begin with.

likelihood.title: Choosing a Model From Its Observed Consequences

sources.title: Fisher: On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics (1922)

blocks: Statisticians needed ways to estimate a population's unknown settings from a finite sample. Fisher's 1922 treatment distinguished likelihood from probability when discussing that estimation problem. The observations are known; the proposed population settings vary.

The distinction matters because comparing how well settings explain data does not automatically assign probabilities to those settings. Our seed example makes the comparison visible with only one unknown parameter. It is a teaching model, not a reproduction of Fisher's data.

naive-bayes.title: Classifying Without a Table for Every Combination

sources.title: McCallum and Nigam: A Comparison of Event Models for Naive Bayes Text Classification (1998)

blocks: Text classification made the combination problem particularly visible: a vocabulary can contain thousands of word features, and possible documents cannot be exhaustively tabulated. McCallum and Nigam's 1998 comparison examined different event models for naive Bayes, including binary word occurrence and word counts.

That paper did not invent Bayes' rule or every naive Bayes model. It demonstrated why the way we represent observations matters even within this apparently simple family. We will use invented binary sensor signs, then distinguish that model from counting repeated words.

support-vector-machines.title: Separating Examples That Do Not Cooperate
blocks: A separator that makes no training mistakes may still sit unnecessarily close to observations. Maximum-margin methods made the distance from a boundary part of the fitting problem. Real datasets then posed another difficulty: measurement error and overlapping classes can make perfect separation impossible.

Cortes and Vapnik's 1995 support-vector networks paper allowed the classifier to handle data that could not be separated perfectly. A point could violate the margin, but doing so carried a cost. The model could then balance a wider margin against those violations. We will use small geometric examples to understand that choice; the paper's experiments concerned optical character recognition.

hierarchical-clustering.title: Keeping the Smaller Groups Inside the Larger Ones

sources.title: Ward: Hierarchical Grouping to Optimize an Objective Function (1963)

blocks: Grouping many observations poses a practical search problem: there are too many possible partitions to inspect exhaustively. Ward's 1963 procedure described forming a hierarchy through successive merges chosen by an objective. It made the sequence of grouping decisions part of the result.

Once groups contain several sensors, there is more than one way to decide which groups are closest. Ward's criterion chooses the merge with the smallest increase in within-group squared variation. We will begin with single linkage instead: find the nearest pair with one sensor in each group. That lets us point to the distance responsible for each merge. These criteria can produce different hierarchies.

density-based-clustering.title: Finding Shapes Without Supplying Their Centres

sources.title: Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu: DBSCAN (1996)

blocks: Spatial databases contained clusters with shapes that centre-based partitions did not describe well, together with observations that should be treated as noise. Ester and colleagues introduced DBSCAN in 1996 to address arbitrary-shaped clusters through a density-based definition.

Its local question is whether a neighbourhood contains enough observations. Connected regions of sufficiently dense neighbourhoods form clusters. Our workshop rebuilds that neighbourhood test, then the lesson follows how those local decisions grow into groups. The plotted sensors are invented.

images-as-arrays.title: Making a Picture Available to a Numerical Machine
blocks: In 1957, Russell Kirsch and colleagues at the US National Bureau of Standards produced a digital scan of a photograph. A picture had to become a collection of numerical samples before their computer could process it. The problem was representation before recognition.

Our tiny tray image follows that same requirement, although it is invented and uses modern array conventions. Giving each measurement a row and column lets us select a region, compare neighbours, or apply the same operation across the picture.

image-thresholding.title: Finding a Cutoff Without Inspecting Every Pixel

sources.title: OpenCV: Image Thresholding, including Otsu's method
Otsu: A Threshold Selection Method from Gray-Level Histograms (1979)

blocks: Thresholding already offered a way to separate image regions, but choosing the cutoff by hand was another problem. Otsu's 1979 method chose a threshold from the intensity histogram by comparing the variation within the resulting groups. It was a method for selecting a threshold, not the invention of thresholding itself.

The useful intuition is to seek two reasonably compact intensity groups. That works only when intensity is a suitable way to separate the objects we care about. Shadows or similar foreground and background intensities can defeat a single global cutoff.

morphology.title: Measuring Shapes in Mineral Images

sources.title: Matheron and Serra: The Birth of Mathematical Morphology

blocks: Matheron and Serra's account traces mathematical morphology to their work in 1964 on the structure of mineral samples. Knowing the amount of a material was not enough; its spatial distribution and sizes mattered. They investigated how chosen shapes could probe the structures in an image.

The shape used to probe an image is a structuring element, also called a footprint. Its geometry determines what an operation considers small, connected, or wide enough. Our seed mask is an invented example of that idea, not a claim that one footprint can distinguish all noise from all objects.

connected-components.title: Following Regions Through a Digital Picture

sources.title: Rosenfeld and Pfaltz: Sequential Operations in Digital Picture Processing (1966), NASA record

blocks: Rosenfeld and Pfaltz's 1966 work addressed sequential operations on digital pictures, including the organisation of picture regions. A computer needs explicit local relationships where a person might simply see a connected shape.

Modern connected-component routines expose the same essential choice: which neighbouring positions may connect? We will use a simple flood fill so every step is visible. It illustrates the task, rather than reproducing the historical paper's algorithm.

image-augmentation.title: Showing a Model Variations of Its Training Examples

sources.title: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (2012)

blocks: The 2012 AlexNet paper used transformations including crops and horizontal reflections to expand the appearances shown during training. The network had many parameters, and presenting only a fixed view of each training photograph made overfitting a serious concern. This was an influential use of augmentation, not its invention.

The reasoning is that some changes to a photograph should leave its target answer intact. We use that prior knowledge to create additional training views. Our small grid example makes the label-preservation requirement visible before any network is fitted.

transfer-learning.title: Testing Which Learned Features Transfer

sources.title: Yosinski et al.: How Transferable Are Features in Deep Neural Networks? (2014)
PyTorch: Transfer Learning for Computer Vision

blocks: Training a deep model for each new task can require more labelled examples than we have. Yosinski and colleagues studied transfer between image tasks in 2014, examining the difference between more general early features and more task-specific later features. Their results also showed that transfer depends on the relationship between tasks.

That work investigated transfer rather than inventing the general idea of reusing learned knowledge. For our purposes, it suggests a practical question: do the available features already separate our new classes, or does the representation itself need to change?

bounding-boxes.title: Comparing Where Systems Said an Object Was

sources.title: PASCAL VOC 2005: Detection Task and Evaluation

blocks: The PASCAL VOC challenge, beginning in 2005, distinguished recognising an object's presence from predicting its location. The detection task supplied labelled bounding boxes and evaluated predicted boxes through their overlap with the annotations. Shared data and evaluation rules made systems easier to compare.

That challenge did not invent rectangles or overlap. It illustrates why detection needs a localisation criterion in addition to a class score. We will use continuous rectangle boundaries; always check a dataset's coordinate convention before applying the same arithmetic to its annotations.

non-maximum-suppression.title: Making Duplicate Detections Count as Errors

sources.title: PASCAL VOC 2005: Detection Task and Evaluation

blocks: The PASCAL VOC 2005 detection rules counted repeated detections of one object as false detections after the first match. Reporting many plausible rectangles was therefore different from finding many objects. Systems needed a way to resolve competing candidates.

Greedy non-maximum suppression is one commonly used procedure for that job. This example connects the method to a documented evaluation problem without claiming that the VOC challenge invented it. The procedure makes a local decision about overlaps; it does not establish the true number of objects.

forecasting-baselines.title: Giving a Forecast a Reference to Beat

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: The Forecaster's Toolbox

blocks: Forecasting grew around decisions that had to be made before demand, production, or other measurements were known. A method needed to earn its complexity against forecasts available from the existing record. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's forecasting text formalises simple rules as benchmarks in this workflow.

We will begin by predicting that tomorrow's demand equals the latest observed demand. This is a naive, or persistence, forecast. Our greenhouse record is invented so we can check every prediction. A more complicated method should be compared with this rule on the same future days.

lagged-features.title: Turning Delayed Effects Into Predictors
blocks: Many processes respond after a delay: an earlier input can influence a later outcome. Dynamic regression includes lagged predictors to represent that timing. The important modelling choice is which past information was available and which delay it could plausibly have.
Our first example uses earlier demand to predict later demand. This constructs a supervised table from a time record; it does not establish that an earlier reading causes the next one.

seasonality-and-differencing.title: Describing Changes When Levels Would Not Sit Still
blocks: Time-series modelling developed tools for records whose levels or recurring patterns changed over time. Differencing became a central part of the Box-Jenkins ARIMA approach: model changes when a more stable relationship can be expressed there.

Let's try differencing on a record where we know the trend and repeating cycle we put into it. We can watch what each subtraction removes. A real record may retain changing behaviour afterwards, so differencing is something to inspect, not an automatic guarantee of stationarity.

exponential-smoothing.title: Maintaining a Level Estimate as Observations Arrive
blocks: Exponential smoothing emerged in forecasting work in the 1950s, including contributions associated with Brown and Holt. Forecasters needed practical updates for changing records, rather than repeatedly treating every old observation equally.

Simple exponential smoothing maintains a level. More elaborate versions add trend and seasonal states. We begin with the level-only update so its response to a new observation is visible before adding those components.

autoregressive-forecasting.title: Predicting a Record From Earlier Values of Itself

sources.title: Yule: On a Method of Investigating Periodicities in Disturbed Series (1927)

blocks: Yule's 1927 work investigated disturbed periodic series by relating a value to earlier values of the same process. That gives us a way to learn how earlier readings contribute, while leaving a remainder for variation the relationship does not explain. We will use that idea with Botie's demand history.

Later ARIMA methods combined autoregressive terms with other components, including differencing. Our exercise fits a small autoregression directly with least squares; it is not an automatic ARIMA-selection procedure.

rolling-forecast-validation.title: Replaying Earlier Forecast Origins

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: The Forecaster's Toolbox
Tashman: Out-of-Sample Tests of Forecasting Accuracy (2000)

blocks: Forecasting researchers needed evaluations that respected the order in which observations became available. Tashman's 2000 review discussed out-of-sample testing choices, including rolling origins, rather than treating one fitted historical curve as evidence of future accuracy.

Let's replay the decision at several earlier dates. At each date we expose only the observations that would have been available then, fit the procedure, and record its forecast before checking the later result. The small arrays let us inspect these time boundaries directly.

exploration-and-bandits.title: Experiments Whose Choices Affect What We Learn

sources.title: Robbins: Some Aspects of the Sequential Design of Experiments (1952)
