blocks: Robbins's 1952 work on sequential experimental design helped formalise problems in which the next experiment depends on what earlier experiments revealed. Sampling a treatment gathers information, but the chosen treatment also determines the outcome received during that trial.

A multi-armed bandit isolates this exploration problem. Our schedules and numerical rewards are invented. Real watering changes future soil conditions, so the independent-trial bandit is only an initial simplification.

states-actions-and-transitions.title: Planning With a State That Changes After Each Choice

sources.title: Bellman: The Theory of Dynamic Programming (1954)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Dynamic programming developed a way to solve multistage decisions by describing the current situation and the remaining problem. Bellman's work in the 1950s made this recursive view central to sequential planning.

A Markov decision process supplies states, actions, transitions, and rewards. Our dry-or-moist greenhouse is a deliberately simplified model. Its value is that every transition can be inspected, not that two labels fully describe soil behaviour.

discounted-returns.title: Connecting Immediate Feedback to Later Outcomes

sources.title: Sutton: Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences (1988)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Sequential prediction needed to account for outcomes that arrive after several intermediate steps. Sutton's 1988 work developed temporal-difference learning, where later predictions help improve earlier predictions before a final outcome is available.

Before using that update, we need to define the quantity predicted. A discounted return combines future rewards with a stated time convention. Our short watering episode makes the accumulation explicit.

bellman-value-iteration.title: Reusing the Remaining Decision Problem

sources.title: Bellman: The Theory of Dynamic Programming (1954)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Bellman's dynamic-programming approach expressed a multistage problem through an immediate choice and the problem remaining afterward. A state's value summarises that remaining problem, avoiding a separate calculation for every history that reaches it.
Value iteration repeatedly applies an optimality update under a known model. Our finite teaching environment separates this planning calculation from learning an unknown model through interaction.

q-learning.title: Replacing a Known Model With Sampled Transitions
blocks: Watkins and Dayan's 1992 paper analysed Q-learning, a method for learning action values from experience without requiring an explicit transition model. It combines an observed reward with a current estimate of the best available continuation.

This belongs to temporal-difference learning: an estimate is moved toward a target partly built from another estimate. Our tabular examples expose the update, including the important exception when a transition ends the episode.

distributions-and-expectations.title: From Games of Chance to Decisions Under Uncertainty

sources.title: Bayes: An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763)

blocks: Early probability problems asked how to reason about uncertain outcomes in games and repeated trials. Bayes’s posthumously published 1763 essay addressed the related inverse problem of learning about an unknown chance from observed outcomes.

Before updating an unknown chance, we need a way to describe a known set of possibilities. Our damaged-sensor distribution is an invented discrete example, chosen so every outcome and probability can be inspected.

parameter-posteriors.title: Learning About a Chance From Its Outcomes

sources.title: Bayes: An Essay towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763)

blocks: Bayes’s essay asked how observations could inform an unknown probability. That reverses the direction of a calculation that starts with a known chance and predicts possible outcomes.

For repeated binary trials, a Beta prior and Bernoulli likelihood give a convenient update: count failures and non-failures separately. This is a particular model with explicit assumptions, not a claim that every uncertain rate follows a Beta distribution.

gaussian-sensor-fusion.title: Following a Quantity Through Noisy Measurements

sources.title: Kalman: A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems (1960)

blocks: Kalman’s 1960 paper recast linear filtering as a recursive estimation problem. An estimate and its uncertainty could be carried forward and corrected as new measurements arrived.

Our thermometers isolate the measurement-combination step. The full Kalman filter also predicts how the state and its uncertainty change over time; averaging simultaneous readings alone is not that complete algorithm.

hidden-state-filtering.title: Combining a State Model With a Measurement Model

sources.title: Rabiner: A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models (1989)

blocks: Rabiner’s 1989 tutorial explained hidden Markov models and their use in speech recognition. A sound recording gives noisy observations of an underlying sequence, rather than a direct label for each state.

We can use the same forward calculation to track the pump. First the transition model tells us how its condition might have changed. We then ask how likely the alarm is under each possible condition and update their probabilities. Our pump example uses supplied transition and alarm probabilities so we can follow each update by hand.

gaussian-process-regression.title: A Distribution Over Functions

sources.title: Rasmussen and Williams: Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning

blocks: Rasmussen and Williams’s 2006 book develops Gaussian processes as a practical framework for regression and classification. A central idea is to describe relationships between function values using a covariance function rather than choose one fixed finite set of coefficients.

For our greenhouse, nearby locations can share information through their covariance. The kernel and noise assumptions decide how far that influence extends and how strongly a reading should constrain a prediction.

minibatch-gradients.title: Trading an Exact Gradient for a Useful Estimate

sources.title: Dive into Deep Learning: Minibatch Stochastic Gradient Descent

blocks: Stochastic optimisation addresses objectives built from many observations by using sampled contributions. Minibatches also make useful work for matrix-oriented hardware without requiring the whole dataset in memory.

This lesson isolates the gradient of a mean squared-error objective with a one-half factor. Our tiny batches make every contribution visible; the same averaging principle applies to gradients obtained through backpropagation.

momentum-updates.title: Keeping Useful Direction Across Steps
blocks: Momentum methods retain information from earlier optimisation steps. This helps explain why a direction that persists can accumulate, while directions that repeatedly reverse can partly cancel.
There are several conventions for scaling the stored state. Here velocity equals beta times the old velocity plus the current gradient; the learning rate is applied when changing the parameter.

adaptive-gradients.title: Remembering Both Direction and Scale

sources.title: Kingma and Ba: Adam (2014 preprint; ICLR 2015)
Duchi, Hazan and Singer: Adaptive Subgradient Methods (2011)

blocks: Adaptive subgradient methods used gradient history to change parameter-specific scales. Kingma and Ba’s Adam combined running first and second moment estimates with a correction for their zero initialisation.
Adam is an update rule, not a substitute for choosing a loss or checking generalisation. Our examples calculate the state explicitly; they do not claim that Adam always outperforms other optimisers.

initialisation-and-gradient-checks.title: Keeping Signals Alive Through Layers

sources.title: Glorot and Bengio: Understanding the Difficulty of Training Deep Feedforward Neural Networks (2010)

blocks: Glorot and Bengio examined why deep feedforward networks were difficult to train, including saturation and how activation and gradient scales changed across layers. Their analysis connected weight initialisation to the number of incoming and outgoing connections.

A finite-difference check addresses a different issue: whether an implemented derivative agrees with the loss. Good initialisation cannot repair a wrong derivative, so our lesson keeps these two checks separate.

training-diagnostics.title: Treating Training Time as a Choice

sources.title: Dive into Deep Learning: Learning Rate Scheduling

blocks: Learning-rate schedules change how far optimisation moves as training proceeds. They address a practical tension between making early progress and making smaller later adjustments.

Stopping based on validation is a separate model-selection decision. The examples here use fixed recorded curves so we can inspect the choice without confusing changing optimiser settings with an independently evaluated improvement.

popularity-baselines.title: Giving Recommendations a Reference Point

sources.title: Herlocker and colleagues: Evaluating Collaborative Filtering Recommender Systems (2004)

blocks: Research on collaborative-filtering evaluation showed why recommendation quality needs an explicit task and comparison procedure. Predicting a rating and producing a useful short list are related but different goals.

A popularity list is a useful reference because it can operate without an individual history. Our library examples expose its main limitation: the system’s past display choices affect which interactions it gets to count.

content-based-ranking.title: Using the Description of an Item

sources.title: Salton, Wong and Yang: A Vector Space Model for Automatic Indexing (1975)

blocks: Vector-space information retrieval represented documents using shared term coordinates, allowing a query and a document to be compared numerically. This provides a foundation for using item descriptions in retrieval and recommendation.

Our guides use two hand-labelled topic coordinates so the comparison is inspectable. Real systems may use terms or learned embeddings, but the coordinate meaning and similarity assumptions still matter.

collaborative-filtering.title: Sharing Judgements Across Readers

sources.title: GroupLens: An Open Architecture for Collaborative Filtering of Netnews (1994)

blocks: GroupLens explored collaborative filtering for netnews, using readers’ ratings to help predict which articles others would find interesting. Shared judgements supplied information that the article text alone might not capture.
Our small rating table uses the same broad idea, but the workshop is a transparent neighbourhood calculation rather than a recreation of the original service.

recommendation-factorisation.title: Sharing Information Through Latent Factors

sources.title: Koren, Bell and Volinsky: Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems (2009)

blocks: Koren, Bell and Volinsky described matrix-factorisation methods that became prominent in recommender systems, including work associated with the Netflix Prize. Learned low-dimensional factors allowed user and item information to interact.
The coordinates are learned to fit the objective. They should not automatically be labelled with human interests such as humour or difficulty unless additional evidence supports that interpretation.

ranking-evaluation.title: Evaluating the Recommendation Task

sources.title: Herlocker and colleagues: Evaluating Collaborative Filtering Recommender Systems (2004)

blocks: Herlocker and colleagues emphasised that evaluating a recommender involves the user task, data, metrics, and experimental design. A numerical comparison is meaningful only when these choices match the intended use.
Our exercise fixes the candidate set, relevance labels, and list length. That lets us calculate exactly what a metric rewards before drawing conclusions about a live recommendation system.

robust-anomaly-scores.title: Estimating a Reference Despite Contamination

sources.title: Huber: Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter (1964)

blocks: Huber’s work formalised robust estimation under departures from an assumed model. The practical concern is that a few contaminated observations should not determine an entire estimate.
Our median and median-absolute-deviation score is a simple robust teaching example, not Huber’s specific estimator. It lets us inspect how the reference changes when an extreme reading is present.

local-density-anomalies.title: Outliers Relative to Their Surroundings

sources.title: Breunig, Kriegel, Ng and Sander: LOF (2000)

blocks: The LOF paper introduced a degree of outlierness based on local density rather than a single global distance threshold. Its comparison lets regions with different densities provide their own local reference.

Our one-dimensional example avoids distance ties to expose the mechanism. The original neighbourhood definition includes ties at the kth-neighbour distance, which can make a neighbourhood contain more than k points.

isolation-forests.title: Detecting by Isolation Rather Than Density

sources.title: Liu, Ting and Zhou: Isolation Forest

blocks: Liu, Ting and Zhou developed isolation-based anomaly detection, using random partitions to separate observations. The method estimates how easily a point can be isolated without first fitting a full density.

Our first tree has supplied splits so every branch can be followed. The second exercise averages path lengths from several trees. A production forest fits many random trees on subsamples and handles depth limits and unresolved leaves.

reconstruction-alerts.title: Using Reconstruction as Evidence

sources.title: Hinton and Salakhutdinov: Reducing the Dimensionality of Data with Neural Networks (2006)

blocks: Hinton and Salakhutdinov demonstrated learning compact representations with neural networks by reconstructing data. A reconstruction objective teaches what information must survive compression.
Using reconstruction error as an anomaly signal is an additional modelling choice. A network may reconstruct some anomalies well, and a normal condition absent from training may reconstruct poorly.

graph-representations.title: Using Relationships Alongside Measurements

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks

blocks: Graph-based learning uses both measurements and the relationships between the things measured. Kipf and Welling’s graph-convolution work provides one influential example of using an adjacency structure to share information between nodes.
Before reaching a learned graph model, we need an unambiguous representation. Our pipe network is an invented example, and an edge records a connection rather than proving a causal effect.

graph-random-walks.title: Ranking Through Linked Structure

sources.title: Page and colleagues: The PageRank Citation Ranking

blocks: PageRank used a random-surfer interpretation to relate the importance of web pages to incoming links from other pages. Teleportation provides a way to leave a local link structure and makes the process less dependent on traps.

Our pipe-network walk first studies ordinary transitions. It is a structural probability calculation, not a physical fluid simulation; actual flow depends on pressures and capacities as well as connectivity.

neighbour-aggregation.title: Learning How to Combine Local Neighbourhoods

sources.title: Hamilton, Ying and Leskovec: Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs

blocks: GraphSAGE learned functions for sampling and aggregating local neighbourhood information, allowing representations to be constructed from node features and neighbourhoods. This differs from storing a separate learned vector for every node identity.

Before adding learned transformations, let's calculate the mean of all a node's neighbours. That smaller operation lets us see exactly which readings reach each node. GraphSAGE also samples neighbours and learns how to combine their information; our first example isolates the gathering step.

graph-convolution.title: A Simple Shared Layer on a Graph

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks

blocks: Kipf and Welling proposed a computationally efficient graph-convolution approach for semi-supervised node classification. Their propagation rule combines self-loops, symmetric degree normalisation, learned feature transforms, and nonlinearities.

The construction here reproduces one forward layer with supplied weights. Training would require a loss on labelled nodes and an explicit split protocol; the forward calculation alone has not learned a classifier.

link-prediction.title: Learning Representations That Support Pairwise Questions

sources.title: Kipf and Welling: Variational Graph Auto-Encoders (2016)

blocks: Variational graph auto-encoders combined graph-based representations with a decoder for reconstructing links. An inner-product decoder provides a simple way to turn two node representations into a link score.

Our exercise uses supplied vectors and the same basic dot-product decoder. It does not implement variational training, and its output should not be assumed calibrated merely because a sigmoid lies between zero and one.

confounding-and-comparisons.title: Making the Intervention Question Explicit
blocks: Causal modelling distinguishes observing a choice from intervening to set it. Pearl’s graphical framework makes assumptions about common causes and pathways explicit, allowing us to ask when observational comparisons identify an intervention effect.
Our plant example is invented. Its purpose is to expose why a common cause of treatment and outcome can distort a comparison, not to establish an agricultural recommendation.

randomised-experiments.title: Defining Effects Through Alternative Outcomes

sources.title: Rubin: Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and Nonrandomized Studies (1974)

blocks: Rubin’s 1974 paper described treatment effects using the outcomes a unit would have under different treatments, and considered both randomised and nonrandomised studies. Randomisation supplies a known assignment mechanism for comparing groups.
We observe only the outcome under the assignment actually received. The example therefore estimates an average difference; it cannot reveal both possible outcomes for an individual bed.

causal-adjustment.title: Choosing Variables by Their Causal Role
blocks: Causal diagrams provide a way to reason about which observed variables should be adjusted for. The back-door criterion addresses common-cause paths that can create association between treatment and outcome without representing the treatment’s effect.

The important step is deciding whether an adjustment set is justified. A numerical standardisation can always be computed from a complete table; a causal interpretation cannot be obtained from arithmetic alone.

treatment-effects-and-overlap.title: Making Observed Groups Represent a Shared Population

sources.title: Hernán and Robins: Causal Inference: What If
Rubin: Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and Nonrandomized Studies (1974)

blocks: The potential-outcomes framework defines an average effect as a comparison of outcomes under two interventions. Hernán and Robins develop identification and estimation methods, including weighting, while making exchangeability, positivity, and consistency assumptions explicit.
Our supplied propensity scores are part of a teaching model. Estimating them from observations adds uncertainty and model dependence; weighting does not automatically remove unmeasured confounding.

saving-fitted-pipelines.title: The Model Is One Part of the System

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Sculley and colleagues described dependencies and maintenance costs around machine-learning models, including the surrounding data and configuration. Those dependencies explain why copying only fitted coefficients is often insufficient.

Persistence documentation also distinguishes numerical model state from its execution environment. Our small JSON example makes the state explicit; it does not promise that arbitrary model objects can be safely or portably loaded.

prediction-input-contracts.title: Treating Data Expectations as Testable Rules
blocks: Production guidance draws attention to training-serving differences and data dependencies. Data-validation pipelines make expectations about incoming records explicit rather than waiting for a model failure to reveal a changed input.
The tiny contract here checks names, shape, and finite values. A real schema also needs units and domain-specific constraints that cannot be inferred from an array’s dtype.

serving-predictions.title: Reducing Differences Between Training and Serving
blocks: Production experience collected in Rules of Machine Learning includes checking differences between training and serving features. A model can behave unexpectedly even when its parameter file is correct if the surrounding computation changes.
Our browser exercise does not deploy a server. It tests the core prediction procedure that an API could call, separating numerical correctness from network transport and operational concerns.

model-versioning.title: Preserving the Dependencies of a Prediction

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Work on technical debt in machine-learning systems describes how data and configuration dependencies complicate maintenance. A model’s behaviour depends on more than the source code of its prediction function.

Versioning is a software-engineering response to that practical problem. Our exercise uses immutable example manifests and comparison fixtures; it does not claim that a filename or checksum alone documents the whole experiment.

monitoring-and-rollback.title: Testing a System That Keeps Receiving New Data

sources.title: Breck and colleagues: The ML Test Score (2017)

blocks: The ML Test Score organised tests and monitoring for production machine-learning systems, including data, models, infrastructure, and changes between training and serving. This reflects a practical reality: model code can remain unchanged while its operating conditions move.
Our small monitoring examples distinguish a changed input distribution from an observed increase in prediction error. Neither should be mistaken for the other.

project-sensor-investigation.title: From Robust Estimates to an Investigation Procedure

sources.title: Huber: Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter
Breck and colleagues: The ML Test Score

blocks: Robust estimation addresses how unusual observations affect a reference. Production testing adds another concern: what happens when that reference is used repeatedly on new records.

This project combines those concerns in a teaching workflow. An alert is a request to investigate, while a fault label comes from a separate inspection. Keeping those meanings distinct prevents the detector from becoming its own source of truth.

project-demand-forecast.title: Evaluating Predictions at the Time They Could Have Been Made

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: Forecasting Principles and Practice

blocks: Forecast evaluation asks what information would have been available at each prediction time. Rolling-origin evaluation recreates that boundary repeatedly rather than randomly mixing earlier and later observations.
Our demand sequence is synthetic and intentionally simple. It provides a testable implementation of the boundary, not evidence that a one-lag linear model is sufficient for real water planning.

project-seed-counting.title: Turning Pixel Regions Into Measurable Objects

sources.title: Rosenfeld and Pfaltz: Sequential Operations in Digital Picture Processing (1966)

blocks: Early digital picture-processing work described operations that inspect pixel neighbourhoods and identify connected structures. Connectivity turns a mask of individual foreground pixels into regions that can be measured.

Our tray uses invented grayscale pixels and a simple four-neighbour rule. A region is an image structure; interpreting it as one seed requires additional assumptions about separation, lighting, and noise.

design-from-decisions.title: A Requirement Has to Describe Something People Need

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: System Design Processes

blocks: Engineers working on large systems have to translate a broad request into parts that can be built and tested. NASA’s systems engineering handbook describes a progression from stakeholder expectations to technical requirements and a design. Otherwise, separate teams can each deliver a working component while the assembled system fails the people using it.

We will use that reasoning for an invented pump inspection service. The arithmetic can tell us whether a proposed inspection policy meets stated limits. Whether the predictions are good enough still needs evidence from representative pumps. First principles give us a way to question the design; they do not supply missing measurements.

design-without-a-model.title: Learning Needs Something to Improve On

sources.title: Martin Zinkevich: Rules of Machine Learning

blocks: Google’s Rules of Machine Learning recommends starting without machine learning when the necessary data are not available, and establishing metrics early. A working heuristic can make a service useful while its team learns what the problem actually demands.

For our inspection service, the temperature rule provides that first comparison. We will assign invented costs to missed faults and inspections. Those values explain the calculation; a real maintenance team would need to justify its own costs and any limits that cannot be traded away.

design-information-boundaries.title: A Model Inherits Its Data Dependencies

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Production ML systems often depend on data produced by other systems. Sculley and colleagues described how these dependencies and changes in the surrounding system create maintenance problems that model code alone does not reveal. A field can retain its name while its meaning or availability changes.

Our two-clock example makes one such dependency explicit. Event time describes the measurement; availability time describes when our service could use it. These invented timestamps are a teaching contract, not a guarantee that every database preserves the history needed to reconstruct them.

design-pipeline-capacity.title: Put Numbers Against the Boxes in a Design

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook: Non-Abstract Large System Design

blocks: A diagram can connect services without showing whether any of them can handle the proposed workload. Google’s Non-Abstract Large System Design approach develops concrete resource estimates from a system’s requirements, then revises the design as those estimates expose constraints.

Our image service is a small invented example of that process. We will use ideal stage capacities first. Those estimates help choose what to measure, but contention and scheduling overhead mean a real benchmark can disagree.

design-queues-and-bursts.title: Waiting Work Can Become Another Source of Failure

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

blocks: Google’s account of cascading failures describes how overload can create growing queues, consume resources, and trigger timeouts or retries that make the overload worse. Requests waiting for service are still part of the running system.

Our queue has no timeout or retry yet. That simplification lets us see the accumulation itself. The example uses discrete intervals and invented traffic; it is not a measured latency model of a production server.

design-memory-budget.title: Small Devices Made the Whole Inference Engine Matter
blocks: MCUNet examined neural-network inference on microcontrollers with tight memory and compute limits. Its design combined choices about the network with an inference engine suited to those limits. A useful model had to fit the way the device actually executed it.

Our budget is much simpler. We count parameter storage, an estimated peak activation cost per example, and fixed runtime memory. We are not reproducing MCUNet’s engine or claiming that this linear estimate describes every network.

design-edge-or-cloud.title: Communication Belongs in the Design

sources.title: Satyanarayanan: The Emergence of Edge Computing (2017)

blocks: Satyanarayanan’s discussion of edge computing describes the role of computation close to data sources when latency and bandwidth make distant processing difficult. The location of computation changes how much information has to travel and how long a response takes.

Our inspection example compares a local estimate with a simplified remote path. It does not claim that local computation always wins. A larger remote model may be more useful, and many systems divide work between the device and a server.

design-feasible-tradeoffs.title: A Trade Study Needs Criteria Before a Winner

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: Decision Analysis

blocks: NASA’s discussion of decision analysis describes evaluating alternatives against criteria, documenting assumptions, and examining uncertainty in the comparison. A list of candidate designs does not choose its own priorities; those priorities must come from the problem being solved.

We will use a small table of invented ML evaluation results. Hard limits determine which rows are feasible. Among the remaining rows, we will identify choices that are worse on every reported objective before asking a person to make a trade-off.

design-sensitive-assumptions.title: Measurements Need an Account of Their Uncertainty

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH: Uncertainty Budgets and Sensitivity Coefficients

blocks: Metrology deals with results calculated from measurements that are themselves uncertain. NIST’s handbook describes uncertainty budgets and sensitivity coefficients for tracking how inputs affect a result. Reporting only the final number can conceal which measurement contributes most to its uncertainty.

We will borrow the question about sensitivity, using a simple design comparison. Our scenarios are chosen alternatives for an uncertain cost. They are not a confidence interval, and we will not assign probabilities to them without evidence.

design-prototype-experiments.title: One Change at a Time Can Miss an Interaction
blocks: Experimental design gives engineers ways to learn from planned changes to a process. NIST’s handbook describes factorial designs, which include combinations of factor levels. Those combinations let us investigate whether the effect of one factor depends on another.

Our prototype varies batch size and parameter format. We will calculate a difference of differences in illustrative timing measurements. This is a descriptive contrast, not a complete statistical experiment or a fitted significance test.

design-fallbacks.title: A Busy Service Needs a Defined Reduced Behaviour
blocks: Google’s discussion of overload describes controlling work when a service cannot fulfil every request normally. Admission decisions and degraded responses can prevent excess work from overwhelming the remaining capacity. The useful behaviour depends on which work the service can safely defer or simplify.

For our inspection example, an unusable sensor record routes to review. That is an illustrative policy chosen for this lesson. A real inspection process would need to establish who reviews the case, how soon, and what happens if that route is also unavailable.

design-inspection-review.title: Meeting a Specification and Solving the Problem Need Different Checks

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: Product Realization

blocks: NASA’s product-realisation guidance distinguishes verification against specified requirements from validation against intended use and stakeholder expectations. Both matter: a system can satisfy a written specification that does not adequately describe the real need.

Our capstone verifies two numerical requirements on invented inspection and workload fixtures. It then asks what evidence would validate the service for the maintenance team. Passing the arithmetic is useful, but it cannot demonstrate fewer real breakdowns or an acceptable review workload.

agent-introduction.title: Giving a Language Model a Way to Check

sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, 2022

blocks: ReAct, introduced in 2022, explored interleaving language-model reasoning and actions with observations from an environment. A lookup could supply evidence for the next step instead of leaving the model to continue from its initial information. It was one contribution to language-model agents, not the invention of agents as a whole.

That gives us a useful place to begin: a proposed action is a request to software, and the result becomes new information. We can inspect those boundaries without asking the reader to trust an answer just because it sounds confident.

agent-prompts.title: Examples Became Part of the Request

sources.title: Brown and colleagues: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (2020)

blocks: Adapting a language model to a task once commonly meant collecting labelled examples and updating its parameters. Brown and colleagues investigated a different setting in GPT-3: give the model a task and a small number of demonstrations in its input, then test it without task-specific parameter updates. The examples helped specify the requested behaviour, although success varied across tasks.

That distinction matters here. Writing a prompt changes the input to an existing model; it does not train the model in this lesson. An agent adds software that can let the model select another action after seeing a result. Anthropic’s 2024 engineering article distinguishes this from a workflow whose route is already prescribed in code. We will use that distinction, while remembering that the word agent is used more broadly elsewhere.

agent-structured-outputs.title: Programs Needed a Shared Description of Valid Data
blocks: Programs exchanging JSON need more agreement than “send some JSON.” A schema can specify property names and value types so both sides can detect an incompatible record. JSON Schema distinguishes defining a property from requiring that property, and allows extra properties unless the schema restricts them.

A generated answer has the same interface problem. We will build a small explicit validator and keep its result separate from an asset lookup. This is a teaching subset of validation, not an implementation of the full JSON Schema standard.

agent-tool-contracts.title: A Missing Response Does Not Mean a Missing Action

sources.title: AWS Builders’ Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs

blocks: Distributed services faced uncertain outcomes before language models began selecting tools. The AWS Builders’ Library describes using a caller-provided request identifier to recognise a retry and avoid repeating a side effect. It also discusses the case where an identifier is reused with different parameters, which should not silently become the same request.

ReAct studied language-model interactions that interleave reasoning and actions, allowing observations to affect subsequent steps. Once a proposed action reaches a real service, ordinary service guarantees still matter. Our workshop separates a model’s candidate request from the application checks that decide whether it can proceed.

agent-context.title: A Model Could Read Retrieved Material at Answer Time

sources.title: Lewis and colleagues: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (2020)

blocks: A model’s parameters are an awkward place to keep knowledge that needs checking or updating. Lewis and colleagues studied generation that conditions on retrieved passages, combining a retrieval component with a sequence-to-sequence model. Documents could provide information at answer time instead of requiring every fact to be recovered from model parameters.

Our workshop isolates a later application problem: given ranked candidate passages, which may enter this request and which fit? It does not reproduce the paper’s learned retrieval or training procedure. That separation lets us inspect permission and budgeting mistakes without disguising a deterministic list operation as semantic search.

agent-loops.title: An Observation Could Change the Next Action
blocks: A language model answering from its initial input cannot inspect a tool result that has not arrived yet. ReAct explored sequences that interleave reasoning and actions, letting observations affect the next step. This supplied a concrete way to combine language-based task handling with information gathered during execution.

Our controller is smaller than a full agent implementation. It consumes supplied proposals and results so we can inspect termination behaviour. The workshop does not run a language model or reveal its private reasoning. It shows the operational decisions an application must make around whatever model supplies the proposals.

agent-or-workflow.title: Separating a Predetermined Route from a Model’s Choice

sources.title: Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system

blocks: Once language models could call tools, developers could give them control over a sequence of operations. That raised a practical question: which decisions should remain in ordinary application code? Anthropic’s December 2024 engineering article distinguished predefined workflows from systems in which a model chooses its next operations. It described patterns used in applications, rather than claiming to have invented workflows or software agents.

Think about the maintenance desk. Retrieving a known record already has a route. Investigating a poorly described fault may require looking at a result before deciding what to inspect next. Our examples use invented measurements to make that design choice visible. They are not benchmark results for any provider or framework.

agent-pydantic-ai.title: Making a Model Response Fit an Ordinary Python Application
blocks: Application developers needed model responses that could be checked and passed to other code. The Pydantic team approached that problem through Python types, dependency injection and output validation. Its September 2025 v1 announcement describes those engineering concerns; the reference here uses the current documented interfaces.

The useful idea is familiar from the earlier lessons: make each boundary explicit. A request receives the manual data it may read, a tool exposes an operation, and the final answer must fit a declared structure. Our invented pump-manual example adds a citation check. It does not turn a well-formed sentence into a verified maintenance instruction.

agent-langchain.title: When Every Application Was Rebuilding the Same Loop
blocks: Agent applications repeatedly need to send messages, execute requested tools, and return the results to a model. LangChain’s v1 release organised a higher-level agent interface around create_agent, built on the LangGraph runtime. Middleware gives applications places to intervene in that repeated execution.

Our maintenance assistant makes the reason concrete. A missing manual should produce a bounded unsuccessful search. We will not infer a hard operational limit from a sentence asking the model to stop; we will enforce it in the program that executes calls.

agent-langgraph.title: A Useful Workflow Sometimes Needs to Go Around Again
blocks: A fixed sequence of language-model calls can work until an early step returns insufficient evidence. The application then needs a route back to retrieval, or a pause for a person. LangGraph’s January 2024 introduction described cycles and explicit state machines as a way to control those paths.

For Botie, the state contains the evidence gathered for one maintenance request. A node returns an update, and the application decides how that update changes what was already stored. The workshop builds that merge operation on small invented records before the reference code introduces a paused graph.

agent-human-approval.title: Permission Has to Belong to an Operation

sources.title: Saltzer and Schroeder: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems

blocks: Long before language-model agents, shared computer systems needed to control who could read or change an object. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 account describes protection mechanisms and distinguishes authentication from authorisation. Their discussion also includes requirements for human judgement before granting access.

An inspection assistant adds generated proposals to that old problem. It still needs a trusted component that grants access to a particular operation. Our approval record is a teaching design for binding a decision to a proposal. It is not a claim that a language model, a checkbox or a checkpoint supplies that authority automatically.

agent-mcp.title: A Common Interface for Data Kept in Different Systems
blocks: Assistants could generate text but often lacked a consistent connection to the systems holding a user’s documents and tools. Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024 to standardise those integrations. A service can describe its capabilities through one protocol instead of requiring a separate custom interface for every assistant.

Our invented maintenance service uses that idea to expose manual content. Sharing a protocol does not settle whether a server is trustworthy, which technician may read a record, or whether a proposed action needs approval. Those decisions remain in the host application and the service that owns the data.

agent-prompt-injection.title: When Retrieved Text Became Part of the Instruction Problem
blocks: Retrieval and tool use let assistants answer from material their developers had never seen. That also gave outside authors a route into the model’s context. NIST’s 2025 taxonomy distinguishes direct injection through a submitted prompt from indirect injection carried by an external resource. The distinction describes the route into the system, not whether a particular attack succeeds.

NVIDIA’s 2023 NeMo Guardrails paper describes programmable checks around an LLM conversation. These checks made the stages of a conversation explicit enough to apply different policies. Our maintenance example studies one of those boundaries: a proposed action must remain within application-issued grants even if the model or a screening step is mistaken.

agent-authorization.title: Permission Had to Follow the Object Being Accessed
blocks: Shared computers had to keep one user’s programs from freely using another user’s files. Saltzer and Schroeder’s 1975 paper describes design principles including least privilege, fail-safe defaults and complete mediation. The recurring problem is deciding whether a particular operation on a particular object is allowed.

An agent introduces a new way to propose that operation, but the service still has the same responsibility. In our invented workshop, the model proposes an asset operation while application-owned records establish the caller’s tenant and grants.

agent-data-boundaries.title: Managing Data Meant Following It Beyond the Database
blocks: Keeping a database private does not settle what happens when an application copies its contents to another system. NIST’s January 2020 Privacy Framework organised privacy risk around data processing and the organisations involved in it. That gives us a useful question for an agent: which information leaves each boundary, for what purpose, and under whose controls?

Tools such as Presidio address a narrower part of that problem by identifying and transforming sensitive entities in text and other data. Its documentation explicitly warns that automated detection cannot find every sensitive item. Our workshop begins earlier, with a new record containing only the fields this lookup needs.

agent-output-guardrails.title: A Correct String Can Become an Instruction to Another Program
blocks: Web applications have long had to distinguish text supplied by a user from markup interpreted by a browser. Cross-site scripting demonstrates what happens when that distinction is lost. Generated text introduces another source of untrusted content; the consuming browser still applies its own parsing rules.

Typed validation libraries help applications reject malformed records, while guardrail libraries organise additional checks and their failure actions. Our teaching example keeps the questions visible: are the fields usable, do their identifiers match this request, and will the display treat the content as text? These checks leave the correctness of the inspection advice for a separate review.

agent-retries-and-effects.title: A Lost Reply Was a Problem Before Models Called Tools

sources.title: Amazon Builders’ Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
Amazon Builders’ Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

blocks: Distributed services have long faced the problem of a request whose effect succeeds while its reply is lost. Amazon’s Builders’ Library describes how client request identifiers let a service recognise repeated intent; its idempotent API article was announced in January 2021. An agent calling a work-order service inherits this same communication problem.

The practical idea is to give the intended inspection a stable identity. A repeated delivery of that operation can then recover its earlier result within the receiving service’s documented contract. Our receipt ledger is a teaching model. It does not implement a distributed transaction or promise that every request eventually succeeds.

agent-resource-budgets.title: An Agent Run Inherits the Resource Problems of a Service

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Circuit Breaker pattern
Pydantic AI: Usage limits and cancellation

blocks: Services already needed ways to stop failed dependencies from consuming every available worker. Circuit breakers record a dependency’s health and temporarily prevent new calls when repeated failures make more work unhelpful. The pattern belongs to distributed-service design; adding a model-controlled loop makes its resource consequences easier to overlook.

A model can propose more work than the application can afford to execute. Current agent libraries expose run limits, but their counters and enforcement moments differ. Our lesson uses an explicit reservation ledger so the reader can inspect what was spent, what is still in flight, and what another call would require.

agent-prompt-examples.title: Showing a Task Inside the Input
blocks: The 2020 GPT-3 paper studied tasks presented through instructions and a small number of demonstrations in the model’s input. In that setting, adapting to the task did not require gradient updates during inference. This made the contents of the prompt part of how the task was specified.

For our maintenance desk, that means we can show a supported answer and a request for clarification side by side. It does not guarantee that a model will infer the intended rule. We still have to test what it does with unfamiliar questions.

agent-tracing.title: Following a Request Across Machines
blocks: A slow response was already difficult to explain in distributed services before language-model agents. A request could cross many machines, while each machine kept only its own local record. Google’s 2010 Dapper paper described a tracing system that connected work across those boundaries using related spans.

OpenTelemetry supplies shared instrumentation and propagation conventions for this kind of record. Our assistant has the same practical need: connect a manual search and a model call to the request that caused them. The invented timings below illustrate that relationship; they are not measurements from a deployed assistant.

agent-langfuse.title: The Answer and Its Test Used to Live Apart
blocks: Once teams compare prompt variants, a plain request log leaves out an important question: which variant produced the answer that received a particular judgement? Langfuse’s documented data model connects observations inside a trace and lets experiments connect dataset items with recorded executions. Scores can then refer to the work being judged.

This is an implementation of evidence we already need, rather than a new definition of correctness. In our maintenance example, identifying the run lets us inspect its retrieved manual, the answer and the evaluator when a score looks suspicious.

agent-evaluation-datasets.title: Testing an Interaction Instead of One Answer

sources.title: HELM: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (2022)

blocks: Benchmarks built around isolated answers leave out much of an agent’s work. AgentBench evaluated language models acting through interactive environments, making sequences of decisions part of the task. HELM separately emphasised evaluating models across scenarios and multiple metrics rather than reducing capability to one favourable number.

Our maintenance tests borrow that question about behaviour: what did the system do in the environment it was given? The small cases here are invented regression fixtures, not a reproduction of either benchmark and not evidence about a particular model’s capability.

agent-framework-tests.title: A Test Double Gives Us Control Over One Boundary
blocks: Agent frameworks inherit a familiar software-testing problem: a dependency may be slow, costly or variable when we need a reproducible failure. Pydantic AI provides TestModel and FunctionModel so tests can replace model behaviour. LangChain documents unit tests using mock models alongside tests that call real providers.

The useful idea is control. Supply a known response at the model boundary and check the application’s reaction. Replacing that boundary deliberately removes evidence about the real model, so integration tests and task evaluations still have work to do.

agent-model-judges.title: When Exact Answers Were Too Narrow
blocks: Open-ended assistant answers made evaluation harder because several phrasings could be acceptable. The 2023 MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena study investigated model judges and compared their decisions with human preferences. It also studied problems such as sensitivity to answer position, verbosity and the judge’s own tendencies.

That work gives us a reason to test a judge rather than simply trust its score. Our maintenance task is narrower than a general preference contest: does the answer preserve what this supplied manual requires? A study on conversational preference does not establish reliability on that domain-specific question.

agent-error-analysis.title: An Average Score Cannot Tell Us What to Repair

sources.title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList, 2020

blocks: CheckList, published in 2020, proposed behavioural tests for language systems rather than relying only on aggregate accuracy. Tests could target a capability and probe how behaviour changed when the input changed.

That is useful for our desk because “wrong answer” covers several mechanisms. We can test whether the right manual is retrieved, whether the answer uses it correctly, and whether an approved call reaches the correct service. Each failure gives us a narrower question to investigate.

agent-ablation-experiments.title: Design the Comparison Around the Question
blocks: Experimental design asks how observations can answer a particular question about a process. The NIST/SEMATECH handbook describes choosing a design around the objectives and factors being studied. Agent development has the same difficulty when several parts of a system change together.

An ablation removes or changes a component so we can investigate its contribution. Here the component is the demonstration set. Holding the recorded model, tools, dataset and evaluator fixed makes the comparison more informative, although repeated model runs and uncontrolled service changes can still introduce variation.

agent-release-checks.title: Make a Repeated Experiment Part of the Change
blocks: Software regression tests preserve known requirements while an implementation changes. Model-based systems add variation in generated outputs, so the regression process also needs fixed cases, identified model and prompt versions, and judgements whose limits are understood. Tools such as promptfoo make these comparisons repeatable from a command line and within a continuous-integration job.

Our maintenance release policy combines evidence from the preceding lessons. It is an authored teaching policy, not a universal threshold prescribed by a framework. The important step is deciding the policy before seeing which candidate it favours.

agent-adversarial-evaluations.title: Friendly Test Cases Leave Some Questions Unasked
blocks: Once a model participates in actions and data access, ordinary accuracy examples leave gaps. A test writer needs to deliberately search for ways the application can violate a boundary. NIST’s 2024 Generative AI Profile includes adversarial testing among its measurement activities. It treats testing as part of continuing risk management, rather than a one-time certificate.

Current tools such as promptfoo can generate inputs aimed at a stated policy and apply different attack strategies. Our maintenance example begins with the policy and observed result, so we can understand what such a tool would have to measure. The attempts and outcomes below are invented records, not findings from a live assistant.

agent-incident-response.title: Someone Has to Stop the Effects While Others Investigate

sources.title: Google Site Reliability Workbook: incident response, 2018
Google Site Reliability Workbook: canarying releases, 2018

blocks: Operational incidents often need investigation and coordination at the same time. Google’s 2018 Site Reliability Workbook describes agreed incident roles and working records so the people repairing a service are not also left guessing who is coordinating the response. Its canarying guidance limits initial exposure while comparing a candidate with the existing service.

NIST’s 2025 revision of SP 800-61 places preparation, detection, response and recovery within continuing cybersecurity risk management. We will apply those ideas to an agent with queued tool actions. Its action history matters because replacing the model or prompt cannot undo an effect that has already reached another system.

agent-iteration-project.title: Keeping a Repair From Becoming a New Failure
blocks: Behavioural tests make a discovered mistake repeatable. Experiment datasets then let a team run candidate versions against stored tasks and expectations. Langfuse supports datasets for this kind of comparison; the useful practice is retaining the case, configuration and observed result together.

Our project follows that practice with small visible records. The tools help us organise evidence, but the expected outcome still has to come from the task. A stored score with no clear acceptance rule is difficult to use when the assistant changes.

agent-guardrail-boundaries.title: Software Needed Boundaries Before It Could Choose Its Own Steps

sources.title: NIST Secure Software Development Framework, February 2022

blocks: Software teams have long needed a way to turn a security concern into a development requirement they can check. NIST’s 2022 SSDF organises practices for preparing development work, protecting software and responding to vulnerabilities. That problem remains when a model writes part of the program or chooses which operation to request.

An agent adds a controller whose proposals depend on text and changing context. We can still describe a forbidden consequence precisely: no record from another tenant may be returned, and no public post may be created without its required authorisation. Those statements give us something more useful to test than whether the agent sounded careful.

agent-guardrail-coding.title: Generated Code Still Has to Survive Independent Review
blocks: Code review and regression testing developed to catch changes whose consequences were wider than the author intended. AI-assisted development changes how quickly a proposed patch can be produced; it leaves the need for evidence about that patch intact.

Modern coding assistants also consume material inside the development environment. OWASP’s secure-coding guidance addresses the resulting trust concerns. For our parser, the practical question is who controls the task, who can change the tests, and which identity may eventually merge the result.

agent-guardrail-sandbox.title: A Process Needed Limits on More Than Its Files
blocks: Operating systems developed process and resource isolation so one program would not freely interfere with another. Container runtimes combine mechanisms such as namespaces and control groups, while their configuration determines which host resources remain exposed.

Generated code makes the reason for isolation easy to see: we need to observe what a program does before trusting it. The isolation mechanism and its configuration are part of that experiment. A container with a privileged host mount can invalidate the boundary we thought we had created.

agent-guardrail-supply-chain.title: A Build Needed a Traceable Origin
blocks: Software supply chains grew beyond a single source tree. Builds consume dependencies and configuration, then produce artifacts that may be copied through several systems. SLSA uses provenance to describe where an artifact came from and how it was produced.

For an agent-assisted change, that helps us ask a precise question: does the evidence describe this artifact? Provenance can establish origin under a trusted verification policy. It does not establish that the source code is correct or that the package has no vulnerabilities.

agent-guardrail-mcp-trust.title: A Shared Tool Interface Made Discovery Useful
blocks: MCP standardised an interface through which a host can discover capabilities from different servers. That reduces the need to invent a separate conversation format for every tool integration. The interface describes capabilities; it does not decide which organisations or installed programs your application should trust.

The 2025-11-25 specification includes tool metadata and change notifications. A host therefore needs to account for discovery as an ongoing process. Our example treats changed metadata as a new review event because a description can influence the next model proposal even when the tool’s short name stays the same.

agent-guardrail-mcp-auth.title: Delegation Needed a Destination

sources.title: OAuth security best current practice, RFC 9700

blocks: OAuth addressed delegated access: an application could receive limited authority without handling the resource owner’s password for every service. Experience with real deployments exposed ways credentials could be replayed or accepted in the wrong context. RFC 8725 and RFC 9700 document guidance for those classes of mistake.

MCP’s HTTP authorisation design uses established authorisation mechanisms and resource binding. Our exercise begins after a trusted validator has checked a token, then asks whether its claims belong at this server. It deliberately leaves cryptography to maintained implementations.

agent-guardrail-application-actions.title: Transaction Review Had to Describe the Actual Transaction
blocks: Transaction systems needed people to approve the operation they were actually about to perform. A generic confirmation could be misleading when important fields changed between review and execution. Transaction-authorisation guidance therefore treats the reviewed operation and its server-side enforcement as connected parts of one flow.

Agent frameworks provide ways to pause a proposed tool call and resume after review. That mechanism is useful, but the surrounding application still owns identity, current permission and the transaction. A resumed model conversation is not itself evidence that the reviewed customer and payload remain unchanged.

agent-guardrail-memory-delegation.title: Saving Context Also Saved Its Trust Problem
blocks: Applications used stored state and worker queues long before language-model agents. Persistent state let later work continue without asking for every detail again. It also required ownership, expiry and access rules so one job could not read another job’s private state.

Agent memory introduces a further concern: stored prose can influence later decisions. A summary can preserve an injected instruction while losing the source label that would help someone recognise it. Delegation therefore needs explicit data provenance and current grants, rather than trust inherited from a friendly agent name.

agent-guardrail-release-lab.title: An Evaluation Needed to Observe Actions
blocks: A text-only evaluation can compare an answer with a reference. A tool-using application can also change state before producing that answer, so the observation has to include the actions and their consequences. Traces and receiver records make those intermediate events available for investigation.

Evaluation systems such as Langfuse organise datasets, experiments and scores. They help retain comparisons across revisions, while the application still has to define an appropriate oracle for its permissions and effects. Our release exercise uses explicit allowed-effect records instead of asking a language model to decide whether an unauthorised write was acceptable.

software-feature-contracts.title: A Model Can Depend on More Than Its Code

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: The 2015 technical debt paper describes dependencies in ML systems that are easy to overlook when attention stays on the learning algorithm. Upstream data changes can alter a model without changing its source code.

Our pump example makes one such dependency visible. A schema names the fields and their meaning; an adapter turns an accepted record into the model’s expected representation. This is a small software contract, with a failure we can reproduce.

software-fitted-state.title: Fit Once, Apply the Same Preparation
blocks: scikit-learn’s guidance separates learning a transformation from applying it to unseen data. Inconsistent preprocessing changes the representation a fitted model receives.

An object with a fit method and a transform method gives those actions different names. The design helps only if transform actually preserves fitted state. A method name is not a guarantee; we can test its behaviour.

software-retrieval-shortlists.title: Keeping the Current Best Candidate Close
blocks: A heap maintains a partial ordering with its smallest entry at the root. Python’s heapq documents priority queues and bounded selection as uses of that structure. The whole collection does not have to be fully sorted after every arrival.

For retrieval, a heap of the best k candidates can keep its weakest retained candidate at the root. A stronger arrival replaces it. The data structure reduces selection work; it does not make the retrieval scores more trustworthy.

software-workflow-dependencies.title: Dependencies Outlive a Single Script
blocks: Workflow orchestrators represent tasks and dependencies so work can be scheduled and failures handled explicitly. Airflow calls this structure a directed acyclic graph, or DAG. A dependency says which task results must precede another task.

For an ML run, the graph must also refer to the intended dataset and model versions. The small dependency matrix here explains readiness; it is not a replacement for an orchestrator or an artifact store.

data-partition-statistics.title: Move Summaries Instead of Every Row
blocks: Columnar formats arrange values from the same field together, making analytical scans easier to perform. Arrow documents a common in-memory representation that different tools can exchange. That addresses representation; distributing a calculation still requires a summary that can be merged correctly.
Our invented training files demonstrate why a mean alone is insufficient. Keeping counts lets a small partition remain small when the summaries are combined.

data-asof-features.title: Historical Retrieval Needs a Time Boundary
blocks: Feature stores provide historical retrieval so training rows can use features associated with their own timestamps. Feast describes searching backward from each entity timestamp within a feature’s time-to-live.

Event-time selection alone may not reconstruct what a service knew. Our lesson explicitly adds an availability timestamp, then selects among records that pass both cutoffs. That extra rule is part of our contract; it should not be assumed to come automatically from any product labelled point-in-time.

data-contract-quarantine.title: Checking Data Before Fitting
blocks: TensorFlow Data Validation compares incoming data statistics with a schema and reports anomalies. The practical motivation is that a training pipeline can execute normally on a dataset whose meaning or distribution changed.

Our example keeps the rule deliberately small: a numeric interval and a rejection-rate limit. A real contract also records types, units and identities, and a monitoring policy needs to distinguish legitimate change from producer errors.

data-stream-windows.title: Streaming Systems Cannot Wait for an End of File
blocks: Beam separates event time from processing time and uses watermarks as estimates of event-time progress. Triggers control when results are emitted, while late-data policy determines what happens to records behind that progress estimate.

We will inspect one fixed event-time window. The browser exercise does not implement Beam: it makes window membership and a late arrival visible before an actual streaming system adds state, triggers and recovery.

data-artifact-lineage.title: Track a Run’s Inputs and Outputs
blocks: OpenLineage describes datasets, jobs and runs, with metadata attached through facets. The separation lets a system describe both a reusable job and a particular execution of that job.

We use a smaller manifest to follow a prepared feature artifact. Its identity includes input content, code and configuration. Matching a filename or a successful run status cannot establish those dependencies.

systems-inference-batching.title: Batching Trades Waiting for Shared Computation
blocks: Triton’s dynamic batcher combines requests for stateless models and can delay dispatch to form a batch. Its configuration exposes the trade-off between batch size and queue delay.
Our fixture follows requests already assigned to one batch. It isolates the latency calculation before adding a scheduler, variable tensor shapes or competing model instances.

systems-agent-deadlines.title: A Deadline Follows the Request
blocks: gRPC documents deadlines and propagating them to downstream work. A caller that no longer needs a result should not leave unlimited work consuming resources behind it.
The arithmetic here uses elapsed durations on one clock. Actual cancellation is cooperative: application work and external effects need their own handling even after a request is cancelled.

systems-kv-cache-memory.title: Reusing Attention State Consumes Memory
blocks: The PagedAttention paper addresses memory management for language-model serving, where key/value caches grow and vary across requests. Its design reduces waste from allocation and sharing decisions.
Our lesson calculates the logical tensor storage before allocator overhead. A real server’s measured memory also depends on layout, temporary tensors and its serving implementation.

systems-context-cache.title: A Cache Entry Needs a Reuse Contract
blocks: HTTP caching rules distinguish cache keys, freshness and constraints on reusing responses, including requests carrying authorisation. The broader systems problem is deciding when a prior result is applicable to a new request.

An agent response adds dependencies such as retrieved evidence and model configuration. Our cache-key exercise is an application-level model; it does not claim that HTTP cache headers alone enforce agent permissions.

robot-perception-frames.title: Geometry Connects Separate Sensors

sources.title: Dellaert and Hutchinson: Introduction to Robotics and Perception

blocks: Robotics combines observations with estimates of motion and position. The robotics text’s discussion of localisation and mapping shows why measurements must be related through explicit geometry before they can describe one environment.

Our exercise isolates a known rigid transform. It assumes calibration is already available, so it does not estimate camera pose or solve localisation. It makes the interface between a learned detector and the rest of the robot visible.

robot-observation-latency.title: State Estimation Connects Measurements Across Time
blocks: Robotic motion models describe how state changes between observations. They allow a system to predict forward when sensors and actions occur at different times.
Here we use constant velocity over a short interval. It is a teaching approximation for a conveyor, not a general tracking system or a guarantee that a moving target will remain on that path.

robot-feedback-corrections.title: Feedback Uses the Result of the Last Action
blocks: Feedback control compares a measured output with a desired value and changes the input accordingly. Proportional action is one part of the PID family described by Åström and Murray.

A learned perception model can supply a measurement or target, while a controller handles repeated correction. The distinction matters: improving a detector’s static accuracy does not automatically establish the stability of the complete action loop.

robot-actuator-windup.title: Integral Action Needs to Know About Saturation
blocks: Åström and Murray describe integral windup when actuator saturation prevents the requested input from being applied. Anti-windup methods use that mismatch to limit or correct the controller’s stored integral contribution.

We implement one discrete back-calculation step for a PI controller. The derivative part of PID is discussed separately from this exercise so its noise and timing behaviour are not hidden inside the same formula.

security-retrieval-authority.title: Authorisation Is a Service Responsibility
blocks: OWASP’s authorisation guidance recommends denying by default and validating permissions on every request. Those principles apply when the requester is an agent application as well as when a person clicks a button.

Retrieval adds an easily confused signal: similarity. Our example deliberately gives the forbidden passage the highest relevance, so the permission decision cannot hide behind a conveniently low score.

security-private-aggregates.title: A Privacy Claim Needs a Neighbouring-Dataset Definition
blocks: OpenDP describes privacy in terms of transformations, stability and randomised measurements. Bounding contributions is important because unbounded inputs can give one individual unbounded influence over an aggregate.

Our exercise uses a fixed public count and replace-one adjacency: neighbouring datasets differ in one bounded contribution. Other adjacency definitions or multiple rows per person change the sensitivity calculation.

security-model-artifacts.title: Object Reconstruction Can Execute Behaviour
blocks: Python’s pickle documentation warns that malicious pickle data can execute code during unpickling. The format reconstructs Python objects, which is more powerful than simply reading a table of numbers.

ML artifacts may contain weights, preprocessing objects and custom code. Our exercise checks raw bytes against a digest obtained through a trusted channel, without deserialising the artifact. A separate loader policy remains necessary.

simulation-time-steps.title: Approximate a Changing State by Following Its Rate
blocks: Numerical initial-value solvers approximate a state from an initial condition and a rule for its derivative. SciPy exposes several methods with different accuracy and stiffness properties rather than treating one step rule as suitable for every problem.

We begin with explicit Euler so every arithmetic operation is visible. It uses the derivative at the start of the interval throughout that step. This makes a useful teaching method and also makes its approximation error easy to expose.

simulation-paired-trials.title: Simulation Is an Experiment with a Random Input
blocks: A random generator lets a simulation sample conditions and reproduce a development run from controlled random state. Reproducibility is useful when changing a policy because an accidental change in sampled conditions can obscure the comparison.

Pairing policies on shared scenarios is often called using common random numbers. It reduces comparison variance when the paired outcomes move together, but that benefit depends on the system; it is not guaranteed for every coupling.

simulation-system-identification.title: Learning Can Begin with a Physical Model
blocks: The robotics text introduces learning parameters of motion models from observations. This connects physical assumptions with statistical estimation: a model can have a known form while some of its parameters remain unknown.
We estimate one gain through the origin using least squares. That restriction is deliberate. An offset, delay or nonlinear saturation would require a richer model and different evidence.

simulation-transfer-checks.title: Variation Can Help a Model Cross the Reality Gap
blocks: Tobin and colleagues varied rendering conditions when training a visual model in simulation and studied transfer to real images for robotic object localisation. The work addresses dependence on a simulator’s particular appearance.

We apply the broader experimental idea to a deliberately small policy-cost table. Varying dynamics or appearance must follow plausible assumptions for the task. Randomisation does not guarantee transfer to every real condition.
